tool.name: C++
tool.tagline: Fast, zero-overhead systems language for performance-critical software
tool.description: C++ is a compiled, statically typed language that combines low-level control over memory and hardware with high-level abstractions such as classes, templates and the standard library. It powers game engines, browsers, databases, trading systems, embedded devices and machine-learning runtimes. Learning modern C++ (C++20, with C++23 notes) teaches you how software really runs and lets you write code that is both expressive and as fast as the machine allows.

glossary.def: In C++, the starting value given to a variable or object when it is created, as in int x = 5; or int x{5};.
In C++, a lightweight object that looks at data owned by something else, such as std::string_view, without copying it. It must not outlive the data it looks at.
A group of lines of code inside curly braces { }, such as the body of a function, an if or a loop. Variables created inside a block exist only until its closing brace.
The smallest unit of computer data: a single 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte.
When a calculation's result is too big (or too small) for its type to hold. For C++'s signed integers that is undefined behaviour; unsigned ones wrap around to 0.
One of the possible paths a program can take at a decision point, such as the if part or the else part of an if statement.
In C++, to hand an object's contents (such as a vector's memory) over to another object instead of copying them, leaving the source empty but still usable.
To follow a pointer (or iterator) to the value it points at, written *p in C++.
A plain C++ pointer, written T*, as opposed to a smart pointer. It doesn't free anything by itself, so modern code uses it only to look at objects someone else owns.
A way to make other threads wait while one thread uses shared data; in C++ usually a std::mutex held by a std::scoped_lock until the end of a scope.
To create a class from another using inheritance: class Circle : public Shape means Circle derives from Shape and gets all its members.
C++17's std::variant: a value that holds exactly one of a fixed list of types at a time and knows which one it is holding.
Judging a type by what it can do rather than what it is called: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck".
The machine code a compiler produces from one source file, with gaps where it uses code from other files. The linker joins object files into a program.
The step that runs before C++ code is compiled. It handles lines starting with #, for example pasting a header's text into your file for #include.
A file (ending .h or .hpp, or a library name like <iostream>) that tells the compiler what functions and types exist, so other files can use them. It is pasted in with #include.
A mistake C++ makes no promises about, such as reading past the end of an array. The program may crash, give wrong answers or seem fine until a later change; compilers assume it never happens.
The rules for which operator in an expression is worked out first, like multiplication before addition in school maths. Parentheses override it.
In C++, a line that announces a name and its type, like int square(int x);, so code can use it before or without seeing its full body.
Handing a function a copy of an argument, so changes the function makes to it don't affect the caller's original. C++ does this by default.
When the compiler copies a small function's code straight into the place that calls it, so the call itself costs nothing.
An array that can grow and shrink while the program runs, like C++'s std::vector, rather than having a size fixed in advance.
A trick std::string uses: short text (typically up to 15 characters) is stored inside the string object itself, so it needs no separate block of memory.
How a C++ compiler chooses which of several same-named functions a call means, by comparing the argument types with each version's parameters.
In C++, an unnamed value created on the spot, such as the result of a + b or std::string{"x"}, which disappears at the end of the statement that made it.
A reference or pointer to something that no longer exists, for example a variable that was destroyed when its function ended. Using it is undefined behaviour.
Giving a C++ variable its starting value with curly braces, like int x{5};. It works for every type and refuses conversions that would lose information.
A conversion that can lose information, such as storing 3.7 in a whole-number variable (giving 3). Brace initialization refuses it.
A variable that belongs to each object of a struct or class, like the x and y of a point.
A function that belongs to a struct or class and works on one object's data, called with a dot: account.deposit(5). Other languages call it a method.
In C++, a simple struct or array with only public data and no constructors, which you fill in directly with braces in member order: Point p{1, 2};.
C++20 brace syntax that names each member as you fill it in: Point p{.x = 1, .y = 2};.
A class's clean-up function, written ~Name(), that runs automatically when an object is destroyed, for example at the end of its scope.
The part of a C++ constructor after the colon that gives members their starting values: Point(int a) : x{a} {}.
Anything a program must give back when it is done with it: memory, an open file, a network connection, a lock.
The C++ habit of getting a resource in a constructor and giving it back in the destructor, so clean-up happens automatically when the owning object goes away, even on errors.
The number that identifies a location in memory, like a house number on a very long street. A pointer stores one.
Moving a pointer by whole elements, so p + 2 points two elements further along an array. Only valid inside one array.
A list stored as a chain of separate items, each holding a pointer to the next one, so adding in the middle is easy but jumping to the 100th item means walking 100 links.
In C++, the responsibility for destroying an object and freeing its memory once it is no longer needed. Smart pointers and containers make the owner clear.
A C++ class (like std::unique_ptr or std::shared_ptr) that holds a pointer and deletes the object automatically when it is no longer needed.
A member function marked virtual, so that calling it through a base-class reference or pointer runs the version belonging to the object's real, derived class.
Copying a derived-class object into a plain base-class variable, which keeps only the base part and loses the derived data and behaviour.
A hidden table each class with virtual functions has, listing which version of each function to run. Objects point to their class's table.
A function that isn't a member of a class but is allowed, by a friend declaration inside the class, to use its private members.
C++20's <=> operator, which answers "less, equal or greater" in one go. Defaulting it gives a type all the usual comparisons.
A C++ enum written enum class: its value names must be written with the type's name (Level::Warn) and don't turn into plain numbers by accident.
The whole-number type an enum's values are stored as, such as int or a one-byte std::uint8_t.
A way to describe how an operation's time grows with the amount of data: O(1) stays the same, O(log n) grows very slowly, O(n) grows in step with the data.
C++17 syntax that unpacks a pair or struct into separate named variables in one line: auto [key, value] = entry;.
A range that includes its start but not its end, written [begin, end). C++ uses them everywhere; an empty range has begin equal to end.
The group an iterator belongs to by what moves it supports: only forward, forward and back, or jumping by any amount. It decides which algorithms accept it.
When changing a container (say, adding or erasing elements) makes existing iterators, pointers or references into it point to the wrong place or to freed memory.
Anything you can call like a function: a function, a lambda, or an object whose class defines operator().
What a C++ lambda takes from the surrounding code: the square brackets at its start list which outside variables it may use, and whether it copies them or refers to the originals.
A C++ lambda with auto parameters, so it accepts arguments of any type.
Hiding many different concrete types behind one common type, as std::function does for anything callable with the right arguments.
A function that tells an algorithm like sort whether one element should come before another.
The rule a comparator must follow: it must answer false when comparing an element with itself or with an equal one, as < does and <= doesn't.
The two-step C++ pattern for deleting matching elements: std::remove_if moves the kept ones to the front, then the container's erase cuts off the rest.
An extra argument to C++ standard algorithms, such as std::execution::par, that lets them split the work across several CPU cores.
One .cpp file plus every header pasted into it by #include: the chunk a C++ compiler compiles in one go.
Lines at the top of a header (usually #pragma once) that stop it being pasted into the same file twice.
The C++ rule that each function or variable may be defined only once in a whole program, unless it's marked inline, in which case every copy must be identical.
Whether a name in one C++ file can be seen from other files (external linkage) or only inside its own file (internal linkage).
A namespace written without a name, namespace { ... }, whose contents can only be used inside that one .cpp file.
What happens when an exception leaves functions on its way to a catch: each function is exited and its local objects are destroyed, in reverse order.
A promise about the state a function leaves things in if an exception passes through: nothing leaks (basic), nothing changed at all (strong), or it never fails (nothrow).
Something a CMake build produces, such as a program or a library, with its own source files and settings.
Keeping all generated build files in a separate folder (like build/) instead of mixing them with your source code.
C++'s way of handing over a resource (such as a vector's memory) from one object to another instead of copying it, when the source isn't needed any more.
An expression that names something with a lasting place in memory, like a variable x or v[0].
An expression that is a temporary value without a lasting name, like f() or a + b, which is about to disappear.
A reference written T&& that binds only to temporaries (rvalues), so a function can tell it may take over their contents.
The constructor C++ uses to make a new object as a copy of an existing one, written T(const T&).
The constructor C++ uses to make a new object by taking over another object's resources, written T(T&&), leaving the source empty.
The condition of an object after its contents were moved away: still safe to destroy or assign a new value to, but its value is not something to rely on.
When the compiler builds a returned object directly in the caller's variable, skipping a copy or move entirely.
The functions C++ can write for a class automatically: default constructor, destructor, copy constructor and assignment, and move constructor and assignment.
The C++ guideline that a class needing a custom destructor almost always needs custom copy and move operations too, so define or forbid all five together.
The C++ guideline to let members such as std::string, std::vector and std::unique_ptr manage resources, so a class needs none of the special member functions written by hand.
Writing assignment by taking the new value as a copy and swapping contents with it, so one function handles copy and move assignment and a failure leaves the target untouched.
A C++ function written once with a placeholder type, from which the compiler makes a real function for each type you call it with.
A C++ class written with placeholder types, like std::vector<T>, from which the compiler makes a real class for each type you use.
C++17 feature that works out a class template's types from the constructor's arguments, so std::pair p{1, 2.5}; needs no <int, double>.
A template parameter that is a value known at compile time, such as a size, instead of a type: template <std::size_t N>.
A C++ template that accepts any number of arguments, written with ... as in template <typename... Ts>.
C++17 syntax that combines all the arguments of a variadic template with one operator, like (xs + ...) to add them all up.
A T&& parameter whose T is worked out from the call; it binds to anything, and std::forward passes the argument on exactly as it came in.
A separate version of a C++ template for particular arguments, used instead of the general pattern when those arguments are given.
In C++20, a named compile-time test on a type, such as std::integral, used to limit which types a template accepts and to give clear errors.
In C++, a condition on a template's types, written with concepts or requires, that must hold for the template to be used.
C++20 syntax listing operations a type must support, like requires(T s) { s.area(); }, used to define concepts.
When one C++ constraint includes another (A && B includes A), so the compiler prefers the more specific, more constrained overload.
In C++ ranges, a function applied to each element before an algorithm compares it, such as sorting people by their age member.
In C++20, a lightweight range that doesn't own elements but produces them on demand from another range, such as views::filter or views::transform.
An expression the compiler can work out completely while compiling, such as 3 * 4 or a call to a constexpr function with constant arguments.
A C++20 consteval function: every call to it must be worked out while compiling, never while the program runs.
A special value that stands for "none" or "not found", such as -1 for a missing position. Easy to forget to check for.
A value that holds one of several possible types at a time and remembers which one, like std::variant.
A tool that lets a thread sleep until another thread tells it that something it was waiting for has happened.
The part of a compiler that rewrites your code into faster machine code that behaves the same, as long as the code follows the language rules.
The C++ rule that an object may only be read through a pointer or reference of its own type (with a few exceptions, like char). Breaking it is undefined behaviour.
A compiler option (like -fsanitize=address) that adds checks to a program so it stops with a clear report the moment it does certain illegal things, such as reading freed memory.
Checking source code for likely bugs without running it, using tools such as clang-tidy.
The rules a language sets for what one thread is guaranteed to see of another thread's writes to memory.
The ordering rule in C++'s memory model: if action A happens-before action B, then everything A wrote is visible to B.
The setting on a C++ atomic operation (such as relaxed, acquire, release or seq_cst) that says how strictly other memory reads and writes are kept in order around it.
An atomic operation that changes a value only if it still equals what you expected, all in one step; the building block of code that coordinates threads without locks.
Describes code that coordinates threads using atomic operations instead of locks, so one slow or paused thread can't hold all the others up.
Using C++ templates to compute with types and constants while compiling, for example choosing an implementation based on a type's properties.
A small C++ template that answers a question about a type at compile time, such as std::is_integral_v<T>, or transforms one type into another.

aliases: substitution failure is not an error
glossary.def: The C++ rule that if plugging types into a template's signature fails, that template is silently skipped instead of causing an error; the basis of older template tricks.
A C++ template technique for asking at compile time whether an expression (such as x.size()) would compile for a given type.
The span between an object being constructed and destroyed. Using an object outside its lifetime is undefined behaviour, even if its bytes are still in memory.
C++ syntax, new (address) T(args), that builds an object in memory you already have, instead of getting new memory.
The rule that a type's address must be a multiple of some number (often its size), because CPUs read aligned data fastest.
Unused filler bytes the compiler puts between or after a struct's members so each member is properly aligned.
The fixed-size chunk (usually 64 bytes) in which a CPU moves data between main memory and its fast caches.
Describes a C++ type with no custom copy, move or destructor, so copying its bytes (with memcpy) makes a valid copy.
Reading the bytes of one type as if they were another type, such as the bits of a float as an integer. In C++ do it with std::bit_cast or memcpy.
The name under which a compiled function or variable is recorded in an object file or library, so the linker can match each use with its definition.
How C++ compilers encode a function's namespace and parameter types into its linker symbol, so same-named overloads get different symbols.
A file of object files (.a or .lib) whose code is copied into each program that uses it when the program is linked.
The machine-level details compiled code relies on: how objects are laid out, how functions are called and how names are encoded. Changing it breaks already-compiled programs.
The agreed rules for where a function call places its arguments and result (which CPU registers or memory), so separately compiled code can call each other.
Hiding a class's data in a separate private struct that the class only points to, so the data can change without changing the class's size or layout.
In C++17, an object that hands out and takes back memory for containers through a common interface, so the strategy can be chosen while the program runs.
A memory strategy that hands out pieces of one big block in order and frees everything at once at the end, making each allocation very cheap.
A memory strategy that keeps ready-made blocks of fixed sizes and reuses freed ones, instead of asking the operating system each time.
The block of memory, usually on the heap, where a paused C++ coroutine keeps the local variables it needs when it carries on.
A small object pointing to a paused C++ coroutine's frame, used to resume it, check whether it has finished, or destroy it.
The object co_await talks to: it decides whether a C++ coroutine should pause, what to do while paused, and what value to give back when it carries on.
Storing each field of many objects in its own array (all x values together, all y values together) instead of storing whole objects one after another.
A slowdown where threads on different CPU cores write separate variables that happen to share a cache line, forcing the cores to keep passing it back and forth.
When the CPU guesses wrongly which way an if will go and has to throw away work it started early, costing a few nanoseconds.
The human-readable text form of machine code, one short instruction per line, which you can read to see what a compiler produced.
A rule about an object's data that must always hold, such as "the balance is never negative". A class keeps its data private so every change goes through code that checks the rule.

concepts.name: Compiling and running
concepts.summary: Turn the C++ text you write into a program your computer can run, and switch on the compiler checks that catch mistakes early.
concepts.why: Every C++ program goes through these steps before it can run, and most confusing build errors make sense once you know them.
concepts.body:
A computer only runs instructions written as numbers in its own language, called **machine code**. Nobody writes that by hand: we write ordinary text in a language like C++ and let a program translate it. The text you write is the **source code**, saved in files ending in `.cpp`.

The translator is a **compiler**. It reads your source code, checks that it follows the rules of C++, and turns it into machine code; that step is called **compiling**. The result is an **executable**: a file you can run, like an app you double-click. The common C++ compilers are GCC (`g++`), Clang (`clang++`) and Microsoft's MSVC (`cl`).

You run a compiler by typing a command in a **terminal**, a text window for typing instructions to the computer. The example's first line compiles `hello.cpp` into a program named `hello`; `./hello` runs it.

Bigger programs are split across many `.cpp` files. The compiler handles each file on its own and writes an **object file** (`.o`, or `.obj` on Windows): machine code with gaps wherever it uses code from another file.

A second tool, the **linker**, joins the object files, plus any **libraries** (collections of ready-made code written by others), into one executable and fills those gaps. So an error like `undefined reference to parse` comes from the linker: it couldn't find the code for something you used.

C++ gets a new version every three years, named after the year: C++20, C++23. Always say which one you want with `-std=c++20`, because compilers otherwise pick an older one. Then ask the compiler for help:

- `-Wall -Wextra` turn on warnings about code that is legal but probably wrong. Treat each one as a **bug**, a mistake that makes a program misbehave.
- `-g` keeps extra information for a **debugger**, a tool that pauses a running program so you can look inside it.
- `-O2` makes the compiler work harder to produce a faster program. Use it for the version you give to users.
- `-fsanitize=address,undefined` adds checks that stop the program with a clear report when it reads or writes data it doesn't own. Use it while developing.

Recompiling only the files that changed is the job of a **build system** such as CMake, covered later. To experiment without installing anything, try the website Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org).
concepts.code:
# hello.cpp contains a main() function
g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -g hello.cpp -o hello
./hello

# while developing: extra checks that report mistakes as the program runs
clang++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined hello.cpp -o hello

# fast version to give to users
g++ -std=c++20 -O2 hello.cpp -o hello

# several files: compile each to an object file, then link them
g++ -std=c++20 -c main.cpp -o main.o
g++ -std=c++20 -c util.cpp -o util.o
g++ main.o util.o -o app

# Windows, Microsoft's compiler (from a "Developer Command Prompt")
cl /std:c++20 /EHsc /W4 hello.cpp
takeaways: Source code -> compiler -> object files -> linker -> executable
Always name the C++ version: `-std=c++20`
While developing, build with `-Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined`
pitfalls: Ignoring warnings: many real bugs, such as using a value before you've set it, show up as warnings first.

quiz.q: You change only util.cpp in a project made of main.cpp and util.cpp. What is the least work needed to rebuild?
options: Recompile util.cpp, then link the object files again
Only link again; the linker recompiles changed files
Recompile util.cpp; no link step is needed
quiz.explain: Each .cpp file is compiled on its own, so only util.o is out of date, but the executable must be linked again to include the new util.o.

quiz.q: The build fails with "undefined reference to `parse(int)'". Which step reported it?
options: The compiler, while checking the rules
quiz.explain: The compiler accepted the code that uses parse; the linker then couldn't find any object file or library containing parse's actual code.

concepts.name: main, input and output
concepts.summary: Write a complete program: the main function, printing with std::cout and reading what the user types with std::cin.
concepts.why: Every program starts in main, and printing and reading text is how you'll try out everything else in this course.
concepts.body:
Every C++ program starts in a **block** of code, a group of lines inside curly braces `{ }`, named `main`: the computer begins at its first line and works downwards. A named block of code like this is a **function**; you'll write your own soon.

When it finishes, `main` hands a whole number back to the **operating system** (Windows, macOS or Linux: the software that starts and runs programs). `0` means success; anything else means something went wrong. That's why it's written `int main()`: `int` means whole number. `main` is the one function where you may leave out `return 0;`, because reaching its closing brace does that for you.

C++ comes with a large **standard library**: ready-made code for printing, text, lists, maths and much more, available without installing anything.

You switch on the parts you need with `#include` lines at the top. Before compiling, a step called the **preprocessor** pastes in the named **header**, a file that tells the compiler what a part of the library offers. `<iostream>` gives you keyboard input and screen output; `<string>` gives you text.

Standard library names start with `std::`. `std` is a **namespace**: a family name that keeps the library's names apart from yours, so your own `cout` could never clash with `std::cout`.

- `std::cout << x` prints `x` on the screen, the program's **standard output**. You can chain it: `std::cout << "a" << 1 << '\n';`.
- `std::cerr` is for error messages (**standard error**), kept separate from normal output.
- Values are kept in **variables**, named places that hold values, like `name` in the example (next lesson). `std::cin >> x` reads one value the user types, stopping at a space or the end of the line, into `x`. If the user types something that doesn't fit, such as letters when a number is expected, reading fails, so check it as the example does.
- `std::getline(std::cin, s)` reads a whole line, spaces included, into a **string**, a piece of text.

`'\n'` is the **newline** character: it ends the line. You'll also see `std::endl`, which ends the line and then forces everything printed so far onto the screen at once. Forcing that thousands of times is slow, so prefer `'\n'`.

C++20 added `std::format("{} is {}", name, age)` (header `<format>`) to fill values into text, and C++23 adds `std::println` to format and print in one go; older code uses `<<`, so learn both. Avoid `using namespace std;` in real projects: it pulls hundreds of names into your file and causes clashes.
takeaways: `main` is where the program starts; returning 0 means success
`<<` prints, `>>` reads one value, `std::getline` reads a whole line
Use `'\n'` instead of `std::endl` unless you need the output shown immediately
C++20 `std::format` and C++23 `std::println` are the modern way to format text
pitfalls: Calling `std::getline` right after `std::cin >> n` and getting an empty string, because the Enter from the previous input was still waiting. Write `std::getline(std::cin >> std::ws, s)` to skip it.

quiz.q: The user types `42 apples` and the program runs `std::cin >> n >> word;`, where n holds a whole number and word holds text. What ends up in word?
quiz.explain: >> skips spaces and reads one value at a time, so n gets 42 and word gets apples.

quiz.q: Why is `'\n'` usually preferred over `std::endl`?
options: endl does not work on Windows
endl also forces the output onto the screen every time, which is slow when done often
'\n' is the only newline that works everywhere
quiz.explain: Both end the line, but std::endl also pushes everything out immediately each time, which costs extra work.

concepts.name: Variables and fundamental types
concepts.summary: Store values in variables of the built-in types (int, double, bool, char and friends) and know their sizes, limits and arithmetic rules.
concepts.why: C++ makes you choose each variable's type, and the rules for sizes, overflow and conversions cause real bugs if you don't know them.
concepts.body:
A variable is a named place in the computer's **memory**, the fast short-term storage where a running program keeps its data. In C++ every variable also has a **type** that says what kind of value fits in it: a whole number, a decimal number, a letter. You write the type first, and it can never change: `int count = 0;` makes a variable named `count` for whole numbers, starting at 0.

Memory is counted in **bytes**. A byte is 8 **bits**, each a single 0 or 1: enough for a number from 0 to 255. The more bytes a type uses, the bigger the numbers it can hold; `sizeof(int)` tells you how many bytes an `int` takes.

The built-in types:

- Whole numbers (**integers**): `short`, `int`, `long`, `long long`. Each has an `unsigned` version that can't be negative but goes twice as high. C++ only promises minimum sizes; on every common computer today `int` is 4 bytes (about plus or minus 2.1 billion) and `long long` is 8.
- `std::size_t`: unsigned, used for sizes and counts.
- Exact sizes from the header `<cstdint>`, such as `std::int32_t` (exactly 32 bits), for when the size must not vary between computers.
- Decimal numbers (**floating-point numbers**): `float` (4 bytes) and the more precise `double` (8 bytes, the usual choice). They're approximate, like 1/3 written as 0.333.
- `bool` holds `true` or `false` (a **boolean**); `char` holds one byte, usually a character such as `'A'`.

A value typed straight into the code, like `42` or `1.5`, is a **literal**. Long numbers may use separators (`1'000'000`), and a letter at the end picks the type: `2.5f` is a `float`, `10u` is unsigned. `std::numeric_limits<int>::max()` (from `<limits>`) gives the largest `int`.

Dividing two integers throws the remainder away (**integer division**): `7 / 2` is `3`. Make one side a decimal, `7 / 2.0`, to get `3.5`. Unsigned numbers wrap around like a car's odometer: `0u - 1` becomes the largest possible value.

Normal (signed) integers don't wrap. Going past the largest `int`, called **overflow**, is **undefined behaviour**: C++ promises nothing about what happens. The program may give a wrong answer, crash, or work today and break with the next compiler. Treat it as a bug you must never write; you'll meet it throughout C++.

A variable created without a value, like `int x;`, holds whatever leftover bits were in that memory, and reading it is undefined behaviour too. Give every variable a starting value, its **initializer**, when you create it. Mark values that should never change `const`: `const double tax_rate = 0.2;`.
takeaways: Sizes vary between computers; use `<cstdint>` types when the exact size matters
Integer division discards the remainder; unsigned wraps around; signed overflow is undefined behaviour
Always give a variable a value when you create it
pitfalls: Reading a variable you never gave a value (`int x; x++;`): it's undefined behaviour, not zero.

quiz.q: What does `int r = 9 / 4 * 2.0;` store in r?
quiz.explain: 9 / 4 is integer division giving 2; times 2.0 is 4.0, and storing that in an int keeps 4.

quiz.q: You add 1 to the largest value an `int` can hold. What does C++ promise?
options: It wraps round to the most negative int
The program stops with an error message
It stays at the largest value
quiz.explain: Overflowing a signed integer is undefined behaviour; only unsigned arithmetic is promised to wrap.

concepts.name: Operators and expressions
concepts.summary: Arithmetic, comparison, logical and bitwise operators, plus the order and conversion rules that trip people up.
concepts.why: Calculations and comparisons are the bulk of any program, and a few C++ operator rules cause classic bugs.
concepts.body:
An **operator** is a sign that does something with values, like `+` or `<`. Values and operators together form an **expression**, a piece of code that works out to a value: `price * 2` or `age >= 18`.

Arithmetic uses `+ - * /` and `%`, the remainder after dividing (`17 % 5` is `2`). Shortcuts like `x += 3` mean `x = x + 3`. With negative numbers, division rounds toward zero: `-7 / 2` is `-3` and `-7 % 2` is `-1`.

`++i` adds one to `i` and gives the new value; `i++` adds one but gives the old value. On a line by themselves they do the same thing; make `++i` your habit, since for some types you'll meet later it's cheaper.

Comparisons (`== != < <= > >=`) give a `bool`. Combine conditions with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not). `&&` and `||` stop as soon as the answer is known, which is called **short-circuit evaluation**: in `count != 0 && total / count > 10`, when `count` is 0 the division never runs. Code relies on this to protect against mistakes like dividing by zero.

The bitwise operators `& | ^ ~ << >>` work on the individual bits (the 0s and 1s) of an integer, for example to pack several on/off flags into one number. Use unsigned types for them.

When one expression has several operators, **operator precedence** decides which goes first, like multiplication before addition in school maths. One C++ surprise: `==` goes before `&`, so `flags & mask == 0` means `flags & (mask == 0)`. When in doubt, add parentheses.

`cond ? a : b` gives `a` if `cond` is true and `b` otherwise: `score >= 60 ? "pass" : "fail"`.

Mixing signed and unsigned integers is the nastiest surprise. C++ first converts the signed one to unsigned, so `-1 < 0u` is **false**: -1 becomes 4294967295. `-Wall` warns about it. It trips people up most often when comparing an `int` with a size from `.size()`, which is unsigned. C++20's `std::cmp_less(a, b)` (header `<utility>`) compares mixed integers correctly.

Finally, `=` stores a value and `==` compares. `if (x = 5)` stores 5 in `x` and then counts as true, which is almost always a bug; the compiler warns about it. (`if` runs code only when a condition holds: next lesson.)
takeaways: `&&` and `||` stop early, so `count != 0 && total / count > 10` is safe
Comparing signed with unsigned converts the signed side: `-1 < 0u` is false
`==` goes before `&`, `|` and `^`: put bit tests in parentheses
pitfalls: Comparing an `int` that may be negative with a `.size()` result; use `std::cmp_less` or make sure the `int` isn't negative.

quiz.q: What does `std::cout << (5 & 4 == 4);` print?
quiz.explain: 4 == 4 is worked out first giving true (1), and 5 & 1 is 1.

quiz.q: After `int i = 3; int j = i++ * 2;`, what are i and j?
quiz.explain: i++ gives the old value 3, so j is 6, and i becomes 4.

concepts.name: Branches and loops
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if and switch, and repeat work with while, do-while, the counting for loop and the range-based for.
concepts.why: Deciding and repeating are the core of every program, and C++ has a few forms (range-for, if with a helper variable) that make them safer.
concepts.body:
Programs make decisions and repeat work. `if (cond) { ... }` runs the code in braces only when the condition is true; add `else if (other) { ... }` and `else { ... }` for the other possibilities. This is a **conditional**, and each possible path through it is a **branch**. Use braces in real code: without them only the next line belongs to the `if`, and adding a second line later is a classic bug.

Since C++17, an `if` can create a helper variable just for itself: `if (int r = n % 3; r == 0) { ... }`. The variable's **scope**, the part of the code where its name can be used, ends with the `if`, so it can't be misused further down.

`switch` chooses between several branches by a whole number or a character: it jumps to the matching `case` label. Careful: unless you write `break`, it carries on into the next label's code ("falls through"). Several labels can share code on purpose; mark deliberate fall-through with `[[fallthrough]];` so the compiler doesn't warn. `default` handles every other value. You can't switch on text.

A **loop** repeats a block of code, and each pass through it is one **iteration**:

- `while (cond) { ... }` checks the condition before each pass; `do { ... } while (cond);` always runs at least once.
- `for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { ... }` is the counting loop: start `i` at 0, keep going while `i < n`, add one after each pass.
- The **range-based for**, `for (int x : {90, 45, 72})`, visits each value of a list in turn. You'll use it constantly with `std::vector`, C++'s list type, a few lessons from now.

`break` leaves the innermost loop (or `switch`) at once, and `continue` skips straight to the next iteration. There's no way to `break` out of two loops, one inside the other, in one go; once you know functions (next lesson), put the loops inside one and use `return`.

Prefer the range-based for whenever you don't need the position number: it can't run past the end. When you do count positions in a list, use `std::size_t` for the counter so it matches the unsigned `.size()`.
takeaways: Use the range-based for to visit every value without counting
`switch` falls through without `break`; mark deliberate fall-through with `[[fallthrough]]`
`if (init; cond)` keeps a helper variable inside the `if`
pitfalls: Forgetting `break` in a switch, so the next label's code runs too.

quiz.q: With `int x = 2;`, what does this print? `switch (x) { case 1: std::cout << 'a'; case 2: std::cout << 'b'; case 3: std::cout << 'c'; break; default: std::cout << 'd'; }`
quiz.explain: Running starts at case 2 and falls through into case 3 until the break.

quiz.q: What does `for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) { if (i == 3) break; std::cout << i; }` print?
quiz.explain: break leaves the loop as soon as i is 3, before printing it, so only 0, 1 and 2 appear.

concepts.name: Functions
concepts.summary: Write your own functions: parameters and arguments, return values, passing by value, and declaring a function before you use it.
concepts.why: Functions let you name a piece of work and reuse it, and C++'s declare-before-use and copy-by-default rules shape how code is organised.
concepts.body:
A function is a named block of code you can run, or **call**, from anywhere, as often as you like. It takes inputs and can hand back a result: `int square(int x) { return x * x; }`. Read it left to right: the result type `int`, the name `square`, then in parentheses the **parameters**, the named inputs (`int x`), then the body in braces.

Call it by writing its name with values in parentheses: `square(5)`. The values you pass in are the **arguments**, and `return` hands back the **return value**, here 25. A function that returns nothing has the result type `void`. A function that promises a result must reach a `return` on every path; falling off the end is undefined behaviour (with `-Wall` the compiler warns).

C++ reads a file from top to bottom, so a function must be **declared** before the code that calls it. A **declaration** is just the first line with a semicolon, `int square(int x);`, promising that the function exists. The definition, with the body, can come later in the file or in another file entirely; the linker connects them. This is exactly how header files work: headers hold declarations, `.cpp` files hold definitions.

Arguments are **passed by value**: the parameter is a fresh copy, so changing it inside the function doesn't affect the caller's variable. Copying a number costs nothing, but copying a large amount of text or data does; a later lesson shows how to avoid that.

A few modern touches:

- `auto f(int x) { return x * 2; }` lets the compiler work out the result type from the `return`.
- `auto f(int x) -> int`, with the result type at the end, means the same and appears in advanced code.
- `[[nodiscard]] int parse(...)` makes the compiler warn when a caller ignores the result, which is useful for results that report errors.

A function may call itself; that's **recursion** (see `factorial` in the example). Every call that hasn't finished yet takes a little room on the **call stack**, the computer's list of which function called which, so recursion thousands of levels deep can run out of room and crash.

Keep functions short, with one job you can describe in a sentence. That costs nothing when the program runs: the compiler copies small functions straight into their callers, which is called **inlining**.
takeaways: Declare before use; the declaration is enough, the body can come later or live elsewhere
Arguments are copied by default
Mark results that callers must check with `[[nodiscard]]`
pitfalls: Forgetting to return a value on some path of a function that promises one: it compiles but is undefined behaviour.

quiz.q: `void reset(int n) { n = 0; }` is called as `reset(count);`. What happens to count?
options: Nothing; reset changed its own copy
Compile error: n can't be changed
quiz.explain: Arguments are passed by value, so only the copy n inside reset is set to 0.

quiz.q: main calls helper(), which is written further down the file with no declaration above main. What happens?
options: The compiler reports that helper was not declared
The linker reports an undefined reference
It compiles; the compiler reads the whole file first
quiz.explain: Names must be declared before they're used in a file; add the declaration `void helper();` above main.

concepts.name: Arrays and std::vector
concepts.summary: Store lists of values: built-in arrays, fixed-size std::array, and std::vector, the growable list you should reach for first.
concepts.why: std::vector is the most-used container in C++; it is the right default for almost any list of things.
concepts.body:
Programs often handle many values of the same kind: test scores, names, prices. An **array** stores them side by side in the computer's memory, each reached by its position number, its **index**. Counting starts at 0, so `a[0]` is the first value and `a[2]` the third.

C++ has **built-in arrays** that come from C, the older language C++ grew out of: `int a[3] = {1, 2, 3};`. Their size is fixed when you compile, they forget it when handed to a function, they can't be copied with `=`, and reading past the end, like `a[10]`, is undefined behaviour. Modern code rarely uses them.

The standard library offers safer **containers**: types whose whole job is to hold a collection of values. You write the element type in angle brackets. `std::array<int, 3>` (header `<array>`) is a fixed-size array that knows its `size()`, can be copied and compared, and costs nothing extra.

`std::vector<int>` (header `<vector>`) is the one you'll use most: a **dynamic array**, one that grows as you add elements. It keeps them side by side in the **heap**, the large area of memory used for data whose size isn't known in advance. A vector comes with functions you call with a dot, like `v.size()`:

- `v.push_back(x)` adds `x` at the end; `v.pop_back()` removes the last element; `v.emplace_back(...)` builds the new element directly inside the vector.
- `size()`, `empty()`, `front()`, `back()`, `clear()`.
- `v[i]` is unchecked, so a bad index is undefined behaviour. `v.at(i)` checks, and on a bad index throws an **exception**: the program abandons the normal flow and jumps to code that deals with the error (the `try`/`catch` in the example), or stops if there is none.
- `v.reserve(n)` sets aside room for `n` elements in advance when you know roughly how many are coming.

When a vector is full it asks for a bigger block of memory (a **memory allocation**), typically 1.5 to 2 times the size, carries the elements over and gives the old block back. Adding at the end is therefore cheap on average. But anything that remembered where an old element lived now points at memory that has been handed back, so don't hold on to an element's location across a `push_back`.

Because the elements sit side by side, the **CPU**, the chip that runs your program, can go through a vector very fast: memory is fetched in chunks, so the next element has usually arrived already. That's why `std::vector` is the right default for almost any list of things.
takeaways: `std::vector` is the default container: elements side by side, fast, growable
`v[i]` is unchecked; `v.at(i)` throws an exception on a bad index
Growing can relocate the elements, so don't keep an element's location across `push_back`
pitfalls: Remembering where an element lives (for example `&v[0]`) and then calling `push_back`, which may relocate the elements and leave you pointing at memory that was handed back.

quiz.q: A vector holds 4 elements and the room it set aside is also full (`capacity()` is 4). You call `v.push_back(5);`. What happens to the elements?
options: They stay exactly where they are
push_back fails because the vector is full
They are probably moved to a new, bigger block of memory
quiz.explain: A full vector must get a bigger block and move its elements there, so any remembered location of an old element is no longer valid.

quiz.q: Which of these has a size fixed when you compile and can be copied with `=`?
quiz.explain: std::array has a fixed size and copies like a value; a built-in array can't be assigned with =, and a vector's size can change while the program runs.

concepts.name: std::string and string_view
concepts.summary: Work with text using std::string, and pass read-only text cheaply with std::string_view.
concepts.why: Text handling is everywhere, and choosing between string, string_view and quoted literals affects both safety and speed.
concepts.body:
Text in C++ lives in a `std::string` (header `<string>`): a sequence of `char`s that can grow, shrink and change. It manages its own memory and behaves like a plain value: copying a string copies its characters, and `==` compares the text.

The everyday operations:

- Join text with `+` and `+=`, which is called **concatenation**: `"Hello, " + name`.
- `size()` counts the characters, `empty()` checks for none, and `s[i]` reads the character at **index** `i`, counting from 0.
- `s.substr(pos, count)` copies out a piece; `s.find("x")` returns where a match starts, or the special value `std::string::npos` if there is none.
- C++20 adds `starts_with` and `ends_with`; C++23 adds `contains`.
- `std::to_string(42)` turns a number into text; `std::stoi("42")` and `std::stod` turn text into a number (and report an error for text like "abc").

Text in quotes, like `"abc"`, is a **string literal**, and surprisingly it is *not* a `std::string`. It's an older, simpler kind of text that comes from C: a fixed run of characters ending in an invisible `'\0'` marker. That's why `"a" + "b"` doesn't compile, while `std::string{"a"} + "b"` works: at least one side must be a real `std::string`.

Short strings (typically up to 15 characters) are stored inside the string itself; longer ones get their own block of memory. This trick, the **small string optimization**, makes short strings cheap.

`std::string_view` (C++17, header `<string_view>`) is a **view**: a lightweight window onto text that someone else owns. It only remembers where the text starts and how long it is. It can look at a `std::string`, a literal or part of either without copying a single character, which makes it the best parameter type for a function that only reads text, like `is_header` in the example. Its `substr` is free too.

The catch: a view doesn't keep the text alive. If the string it looks at is destroyed, the view points at garbage, and reading it is undefined behaviour. Never return a `string_view` into a string created inside the function, and never keep one longer than the string it looks at.

A `char` is one byte, not one letter. Letters beyond plain English, like é or 中, are usually stored as **UTF-8**, the standard way of turning text into bytes, which uses two to four bytes for them. A `std::string` holds UTF-8 fine, but `size()` counts bytes, not letters.
takeaways: `std::string` owns its text; `std::string_view` only looks at someone else's
Take read-only text parameters as `std::string_view`
`find` returns `std::string::npos` when nothing matches
pitfalls: Returning a `std::string_view` that looks into a string created inside the function, which is destroyed when the function ends.

quiz.q: Why doesn't `auto s = "Hello, " + "world";` compile?
options: Quoted literals are plain C text, not std::string, and C++ has no + that joins two of them
auto can't be used with text
quiz.explain: Neither side is a std::string, so there is no + that joins them; make one side a std::string.

quiz.q: Which parameter type lets a read-only function accept a std::string, a quoted literal, or part of either, without copying any characters?
quiz.explain: string_view just remembers where existing text starts and how long it is, so it can look at all of these without copying.

concepts.name: Overloading and default arguments
concepts.summary: Give several functions the same name with different parameter types, and make the last parameters optional with defaults.
concepts.why: Overloading is everywhere in the standard library, and it is the basis for later features like defining what + means for your own types.
concepts.body:
Sometimes one action makes sense for different kinds of input: printing a whole number, a decimal or some text. C++ lets several functions share one name as long as their parameter lists differ. That's **overloading**: `print(3)` and `print(2.5)` call different functions.

At each call the compiler picks the best match, a step called **overload resolution**. Roughly: an exact type match wins; next comes a safe widening, like `char` to `int` or `float` to `double`; then an ordinary **type conversion**, like `int` to `double`; and last a conversion that a library type provides, like quoted text to `std::string`.

Overloads must differ in their parameters. Two functions that differ only in their result type can't both exist, because a call like `f(1)` couldn't tell them apart.

If two candidates are equally good, the call is **ambiguous** and won't compile. The classic example is calling `print(3L)` (the `L` makes it a `long`) when only `print(int)` and `print(double)` exist: converting a `long` to either one is an ordinary conversion, so neither wins. Fix it by converting yourself, `print(static_cast<int>(3L))`, or by adding another overload.

A **default argument** makes the last parameters optional: `pad(std::string s, std::size_t width = 8, char fill = '.')` can be called with one, two or three arguments. Defaults must come at the end of the list, and they belong in the declaration that callers see (usually in the header), not repeated where the function's body is written.

Overload when the functions do the same job for different types, like the standard library's `std::to_string`. If the jobs differ, give them different names. When only one value varies, a default argument is simpler than a second overload. Later you'll learn a way to write one function that the compiler adapts to every type.
takeaways: Overloads must differ in parameters, never only in result type
Exact match beats widening, which beats conversion; a tie is an error
Default arguments go at the end, in the declaration
pitfalls: Repeating the default value both in the header's declaration and where the body is written: that won't compile.

quiz.q: Given only `void f(long)` and `void f(double)`, what does `f(5)` do?
options: It is ambiguous and does not compile
quiz.explain: int to long and int to double are both ordinary conversions of equal rank, so neither overload is better.

quiz.q: Which declaration is valid?
options: void g(int a = 1, int a2 = a);
int g(int a); double g(int a);
quiz.explain: Defaults must be at the end; overloads can't differ only in result type; and a default can't use another parameter.

concepts.name: References
concepts.summary: Use references, second names for existing variables, to pass big values without copying and to let functions change their arguments.
concepts.why: Passing by const reference is the standard way to hand values to functions in C++, and references appear in almost every function you'll read.
concepts.body:
Copying is C++'s default: assigning a variable or passing an argument makes a fresh copy. Often you want the opposite, to work on the original. A **reference** is a second name for an existing variable: after `int& r = a;`, `r` *is* `a`, and reading or writing `r` reads or writes `a`. The `&` after the type makes it a reference.

A reference must be tied to something when it's created and can never be re-tied. `r = b;` doesn't make `r` refer to `b`; it copies `b`'s value into `a`.

References are mostly used for function parameters. There are three common choices, where `T` stands for any type:

- `void f(T& x)`: the function works on the caller's own variable and may change it.
- `void f(const T& x)`: no copy and no changes (`const` means read-only). This is the standard way to pass anything bigger than a number, such as strings and vectors. It also accepts a **temporary**, a value created on the spot just for the call, as in `f(std::string{"tmp"})`.
- `void f(T x)`: by value, for small things like `int` and `double`, or when the function wants its own copy anyway.

In range-based for loops, `for (auto& x : v)` lets you change each element in place, and `for (const auto& x : v)` reads them without copying. (`auto` lets the compiler fill in the element type; a later lesson covers it.)

The big danger is a **dangling reference**: one that outlives the variable it names. The classic case is returning a reference to a **local variable**, one created inside the function. Locals are destroyed when the function returns, so the reference is left naming nothing, and using it is undefined behaviour. Compilers warn about obvious mistakes but not all of them. Returning a reference is fine when the thing lives on, such as an element of a vector the caller owns.

Later you'll meet pointers, which also refer to other values but can be empty and re-aimed. References can't be empty and need no special characters to use, which makes them the default way to say "refer to something that definitely exists".
takeaways: A reference is a second name: tied to something when created, never re-tied
Pass big values as `const T&`, values to change as `T&`, small values by value
Never return a reference to a local variable
pitfalls: Returning a reference (or a `std::string_view`) to a local variable or temporary that is destroyed when the function ends.

quiz.q: After `int x = 1, y = 5; int& r = x; r = y; y = 9;`, what is x?
quiz.explain: r = y copies y's value (5) into x; r still names x, so the later change to y doesn't matter.

quiz.q: Which is the usual way to pass a large std::vector that the function only reads?
quiz.explain: A const reference avoids the copy and tells readers the function won't change the vector.

concepts.name: auto and brace initialization
concepts.summary: Let the compiler work out types with auto, and use brace initialization for safe starting values that never silently lose information.
concepts.why: Modern C++ code uses auto and {} everywhere; knowing their exact rules avoids hidden copies and surprising vector sizes.
concepts.body:
Writing out long types gets tedious. `auto` asks the compiler to work out a variable's type from its starting value: `auto n = 42;` makes an `int`, `auto d = 2.5;` a `double`. This is **type inference**. It shines with long type names and keeps code correct when a type changes somewhere else.

The rule to remember: plain `auto` always makes a fresh copy, losing `const` and `&`. If `ref` is a `const std::vector<int>&`, then `auto v = ref;` copies the whole vector. Write `const auto& v = ref;` for a read-only reference with no copy, or `auto&` when you want to change the original.

C++ has several ways to give a variable its starting value. **Brace initialization**, with curly braces, works everywhere and is the safest:

- `int x{5};` or `int x = {5};`
- `int zero{};`: empty braces give a number `0`, a `bool` `false`, and a string or vector nothing in it.
- Braces refuse **narrowing**, a conversion that loses information: `int n{3.7};` is a **compile error** (the compiler stops and refuses to build the program), while `int n = 3.7;` silently chops the value to `3`.

The big gotcha is with vectors. Parentheses mean "how many, and what value": `std::vector<int> a(3, 7);` is three sevens. Braces mean "exactly these elements": `std::vector<int> b{3, 7};` holds just 3 and 7. Use parentheses when you mean a count.

Another subtle one: `auto s = "hi";` doesn't make a `std::string`. It keeps the string literal's older C type, which has no `.size()` and no `+` for joining. Write `std::string s = "hi";` instead.

Use `auto` where the type is obvious or long and noisy; spell the type out where it tells the reader something useful.
takeaways: `auto` copies and loses `const`/`&`; use `const auto&` to avoid copies
Braces refuse narrowing, and empty braces `{}` give zero
With vectors, braces list the elements: `std::vector<int>{3, 7}` has two
pitfalls: Writing `std::vector<int> v{n};` expecting n elements: it creates one element with the value n.

quiz.q: What is the type of `x` in `const std::string& r = name; auto x = r;`?
quiz.explain: Plain auto drops the reference and the const, so x is a new std::string copy.

quiz.q: How many elements does `std::vector<int> v{5, 0};` contain?
quiz.explain: Braces list the elements, so v holds the two values 5 and 0.

concepts.name: Structs and classes
concepts.summary: Define your own types with struct and class: data members, member functions, public and private, and constructors.
concepts.why: Your own types are how C++ programs model the things they deal with, and the class is the foundation for the rest of the language.
concepts.body:
So far every value has been one number or one piece of text. Real programs handle things made of several parts: a point has an x and a y; a bank account has an owner and a balance. A **struct** or **class** defines your own type that bundles such parts together, and each value of that type is an **object**.

The parts are called members. **Data members** hold the values (`double x = 0;`, with an optional starting value). **Member functions** belong to the type and work on its data; you call them with a dot, `acc.deposit(500)`, just like `name.size()` on a string.

The only difference between the words `struct` and `class` is who may use the members by default. In a struct everything is `public`, usable from anywhere; in a class it's `private`, usable only by the type's own member functions. Both can have `public:` and `private:` sections.

Why hide data? Many types have an **invariant**, a rule that must always hold, such as "the balance only changes through `deposit`, which ignores negative amounts". Keep such data private and offer member functions, so every change goes through code that checks the rule. By convention, use `struct` for plain bundles of data and `class` for types with an invariant.

A member function marked `const` after its parameter list, like `long balance() const`, promises not to change the object. It's the only kind you can call on a `const` object.

A struct with only public data and no constructors is an **aggregate type**: fill it with braces in member order, `Point p{1.5, 2.0};`. C++20 adds **designated initialization**, `Point q{.x = 3, .y = 4};`, which names the members (in order) and may skip some, which then keep their starting values.

A class with an invariant sets itself up in a **constructor**: a member function with the class's name that runs automatically when an object is created. In `Account(std::string owner) : owner_{owner} {}`, the part after the colon gives the members their starting values. Mark one-argument constructors `explicit`, so a plain `std::string` can't silently turn into an `Account`.

Objects are values: `Point b = a;` copies every member, and each object has its own data. Member functions don't make objects bigger; only data members take space.
takeaways: `struct` and `class` differ only in who may use members by default
Keep data private when the type has an invariant; offer member functions instead
Aggregate types take `{...}`; C++20 adds `.member = value`
pitfalls: Making every member public, or adding a pair of functions that read and change each member: that protects nothing. Offer meaningful operations instead.

quiz.q: What is the only language difference between `struct S { int a; };` and `class S { int a; };`?
options: A class can have member functions, a struct cannot
Only a class can be copied
Members are public by default in a struct and private in a class
quiz.explain: Both keywords define the same kind of type; only who may use the members by default differs.

quiz.q: Why mark `long balance() const`?
options: It makes the balance impossible to change anywhere
It lets it be called on const objects and promises not to change the object
It makes the return value const
quiz.explain: A const member function can be called on const objects and can't change the object's data members.

concepts.name: Constructors, destructors and RAII
concepts.summary: Set objects up with constructors, clean up with destructors, and tie every resource to an object's lifetime (RAII).
concepts.why: RAII is the central idea of C++: it is how the language cleans up memory, files and locks automatically, without a garbage collector or manual clean-up code.
concepts.body:
A **constructor** runs when an object is created, and a **destructor**, written `~T()`, runs when it is destroyed. The span between the two is the object's **lifetime**. For a local variable it ends at a predictable moment: at the closing brace of its scope, in reverse order of creation. It also happens when the scope is left early by `return`, `break` or an exception.

Give members their starting values in the **member initializer list**, the part after the colon, `Trace(std::string n) : name_{n} {}`, rather than by assigning in the body. Members are always set up in the order they are declared in the class, whatever order you write the list in, so keep the two the same (`-Wall` warns otherwise). `const` members and reference members can only be set there.

Other constructor tools:

- `T() = default;` keeps the constructor the compiler would write for you; one constructor can hand over to another: `T() : T(0) {}`.
- `explicit` on one-argument constructors prevents surprising automatic conversions.

A **resource** is anything a program must give back when it's done: heap memory, an open file, a network connection, or a **lock** that stops two parts of a program from changing the same data at once. **RAII** ("Resource Acquisition Is Initialization") means: get the resource in a constructor and give it back in the destructor. Because destructors always run when the owning object goes away, the resource can't leak, even when an error cuts a function short.

Many languages instead use a **garbage collector**, a background helper that frees unused memory at some later time, plus manual `close()` calls or special clean-up sections for everything else. C++ needs neither.

The standard library is built this way: `std::vector` and `std::string` free their memory, `std::ofstream` (an output file) closes its file, `std::lock_guard` releases its lock, and `std::unique_ptr` (next lessons) deletes its object.

The rule of thumb: never manage a resource by hand in application code. Wrap it in a class, or use an existing one, and let scope do the clean-up. Destructors must not throw an exception; C++ marks them `noexcept` ("never throws") automatically.
takeaways: Destructors run at scope exit in reverse order, on every path including exceptions
RAII: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor
Members are initialised in declaration order; use the member initializer list
pitfalls: Writing a member initializer list in a different order than the declarations and reading a member before it is initialised.

quiz.q: A function creates `A a; B b; C c;` and then throws an exception. In what order are they destroyed?
options: They are not destroyed because of the exception
quiz.explain: As the exception leaves the function, every local that was fully created is destroyed, in reverse order of creation.

quiz.q: Class X declares `int a; int b;` and its constructor is `X() : b{1}, a{b + 1} {}`. What is wrong?
options: a is set up first, so it reads b before b has a value
b must be listed first in the class
Initializer lists can't use other members
quiz.explain: Members are set up in declaration order, so a{b + 1} runs while b still has no value.

concepts.name: Const correctness
concepts.summary: Mark what must not change with const: variables, reference parameters and member functions, so the compiler enforces it.
concepts.why: Const is a promise the compiler checks; code that marks const correctly is safer, clearer, and works with const objects.
concepts.body:
`const` says "this won't change", and the compiler holds you to it. It appears in three main places.

**Const variables.** `const int max_items = 10;` can't be changed after it is created. Use it by default for values you don't intend to change; it makes code easier to reason about. (For values known while compiling, `constexpr` is even stronger; see the Advanced lessons.)

**Const reference parameters.** `void report(const Inventory& inv)` promises the caller that `inv` won't be changed, and it accepts temporaries and const objects too. (Pointers, a later lesson, have their own `const` rules.)

**Const member functions.** `std::size_t count() const;` means the function doesn't change the object. Only const member functions can be called on a const object or through a const reference. That makes const spread in a good way: if `count()` forgets its `const`, nobody holding a `const Inventory&` can call it. Mark every member function that doesn't change what the object looks like from outside as const.

Getters often come in pairs, a const version returning `const T&` and a non-const version returning `T&`, as `std::vector`'s `[]` does.

Sometimes a const function needs to update something that isn't really part of the object's value: a **cache** (a saved result, kept so it needn't be recomputed) or a statistics counter. Declare such members **mutable**, meaning changeable even inside const functions. Use it sparingly. A const function may be called from several **threads** (parts of a program running at the same time) at once, so mutable members then need protecting with a lock.

Avoid `const_cast`, which strips `const` away; changing an object that was created const is undefined behaviour.
takeaways: Mark every member function that doesn't change the object `const`
Pass read-only parameters as `const T&`
`mutable` is for caches and counters, not for the object's real value
pitfalls: Forgetting `const` on a getter, which makes it impossible to call through any `const&` in the codebase.

quiz.q: `void show(const Widget& w) { w.draw(); }` fails to compile. What is the most likely fix?
options: Change the parameter to Widget w
Declare draw() as a const member function
quiz.explain: Through a const reference only const member functions can be called, so draw() needs to be const if it doesn't change the widget.

quiz.q: A const member function needs to count how often it is called. What is the clean way?
options: Make the counter a mutable member
Store the count in a global variable
quiz.explain: mutable members may change inside const functions; they're meant for counters and caches that aren't part of the object's value.

concepts.name: Pointers
concepts.summary: Understand raw pointers: memory addresses, dereferencing, nullptr, pointer arithmetic, and their modern role of looking at objects others own.
concepts.why: Pointers sit underneath arrays, linked data and code written in C, and you must read them fluently even if you rarely manage memory with them yourself.
concepts.body:
Every byte of memory has a number, its **memory address**, like a house number on a very long street. A **pointer** is a variable that holds an address. `int* p = &x;` stores the address of `x` (`&` here means "address of"); `*p` follows the address to reach `x` itself, which is called to **dereference** the pointer. For a pointer to a struct, `p->member` is shorthand for `(*p).member`.

Unlike references, pointers can be **null**, pointing at nothing (write `nullptr`, never `NULL` or `0` in modern code); they can be re-aimed at something else; and you must dereference them explicitly. Dereferencing a null or dangling pointer is undefined behaviour, so check for `nullptr` wherever "nothing" is allowed.

Pointers and arrays are closely tied. A built-in array's name turns into a pointer to its first element (it "decays"), and **pointer arithmetic** steps by whole elements: `p + 2` points two `int`s further on, and `p[i]` means `*(p + i)`. Arithmetic is only valid within one array (plus one position past the end); going beyond is undefined.

`const` reads right to left: `const T*` is a pointer to something you can't change through it; `T* const` is a pointer that can't be re-aimed.

You can create an object on the heap with `new` and must later free it with `delete` (or `new[]` with `delete[]`). Doing this by hand easily causes a **memory leak**, memory that is never given back, when a function returns early or an exception is thrown, and freeing twice is undefined behaviour. In modern C++ **raw pointers**, plain `T*` as opposed to smart pointers, don't own: containers and smart pointers (next lesson) own memory, and plain pointers or references only look at objects someone else owns.

So when should a function take `T*` instead of `T&`? When "no object" is a valid argument; otherwise a reference states the intent better. Pointers remain essential for a **linked list**, a chain of objects where each holds a pointer to the next, for functions written in C, and for low-level code.
takeaways: `&x` takes an address, `*p` follows it, `p->m` reaches a member
Use `nullptr`; dereferencing null or a dangling pointer is undefined behaviour
Raw pointers look at objects; containers and smart pointers own them
pitfalls: Using `new` and `delete` by hand in application code, leaking memory on an early return or exception.

quiz.explain: p points at a[1], so p[2] is *(p + 2), which is a[3] = 40.

quiz.q: When is a plain `T*` parameter a better choice than `T&`?
options: When passing "no object" (nullptr) is a valid option
When the function needs to modify the object
When the function will delete the object
quiz.explain: References can't be null, so a pointer expresses an optional argument; handing over ownership is a job for a smart pointer.

concepts.name: Smart pointers
concepts.summary: Own heap objects safely with std::unique_ptr, share them with std::shared_ptr, and break cycles with std::weak_ptr.
concepts.why: Smart pointers make it explicit who frees each heap object and do it automatically; they replace almost every use of new and delete.
concepts.body:
**Ownership** means being responsible for destroying an object and freeing its memory. **Smart pointers** (header `<memory>`) are RAII classes that own a heap object and delete it automatically when they go away.

`std::unique_ptr<T>` is **sole ownership**. Create one with `std::make_unique<T>(args...)`. It can't be copied, only handed over: `auto b = std::move(a);` gives ownership to `b` and leaves `a` null (the Move semantics lesson explains `std::move`). Hand-overs are therefore visible in the code. It costs nothing extra compared with a raw pointer, which makes it the default choice. It also handles arrays (`std::unique_ptr<int[]>`) and custom clean-up, for example closing a file opened with C's `fopen`.

`std::shared_ptr<T>` is **shared ownership** through **reference counting**: the object keeps a count of how many `shared_ptr`s point at it; each copy adds one, each destroyed copy subtracts one, and the object is deleted when the count reaches zero. Create it with `std::make_shared<T>(args...)`, which allocates the object and its count together. The count is updated safely even when several threads copy pointers at once (the object itself gets no such protection). That safe update costs a little, so pass a `shared_ptr` by reference, or don't pass it at all when the function doesn't need ownership.

`std::weak_ptr<T>` watches a shared object without keeping it alive. Call `lock()` to get a `shared_ptr` if the object still exists. Use it to break **cycles**: two objects holding `shared_ptr`s to each other never reach a count of zero, so both leak.

Guidelines:

- Prefer `unique_ptr`; use `shared_ptr` only when ownership really is shared.
- Functions that just use an object should take `T&` or `T*`, not a smart pointer.
- Never create two smart pointers from the same raw pointer: each would delete it.
takeaways: `unique_ptr` by default: no extra cost, ownership can be handed over but not copied
`shared_ptr` for genuinely shared ownership; `weak_ptr` to observe and break cycles
Create with `make_unique` / `make_shared`; pass `T&` to functions that don't own
pitfalls: Two objects holding `shared_ptr`s to each other: the cycle keeps both alive forever. Make one side a `weak_ptr`.

quiz.q: What happens with `auto a = std::make_unique<int>(5); auto b = a;`?
options: b gets a deep copy of the int
Compile error: unique_ptr can't be copied
quiz.explain: unique_ptr forbids copying; you must write std::move(a) to hand ownership over.

quiz.q: A function only reads a Texture and doesn't care how it's owned. What should it take?
quiz.explain: A reference works however the object is owned and costs nothing; a smart pointer parameter suggests the function takes part in ownership.

concepts.name: Inheritance and virtual functions
concepts.summary: Build families of related classes with inheritance, let them override virtual functions, and know why base classes need virtual destructors.
concepts.why: Virtual functions let one piece of code work with many related types, as in drawing programs, game objects and plugin systems.
concepts.body:
**Inheritance** builds a new class on top of an existing one. `class Circle : public Shape` makes `Circle` a kind of `Shape`: it gets all of Shape's members and may add its own. `Shape` is the **base class** and `Circle` the **derived class**. A `Circle` can be used wherever a `Shape&` or `Shape*` is expected.

A member function declared `virtual` in the base is a **virtual function**: the version that runs is chosen while the program runs, from the object's real type. Calling `s->area()` through a `Shape*` that actually points at a `Circle` runs `Circle::area`. This is **polymorphism**: one call, different behaviour per type. A derived class that supplies its own version **overrides** the base one; write `override` on it, and the compiler errors if it doesn't actually match a base virtual function, which catches typos and a mismatched `const`.

A function declared `= 0` is **pure virtual**: the base gives no version at all. A class with one is an **abstract class**: you can't create objects of it, only of derived classes, which makes it an **interface**, a list of operations every derived class promises to provide. `final` stops further overriding or deriving.

Three rules that matter in practice:

- Give a base class used this way a **virtual destructor** (`virtual ~Shape() = default;`). Otherwise deleting a derived object through a base pointer, which is exactly what `std::unique_ptr<Shape>` does, is undefined behaviour.
- Polymorphism only works through references and pointers. Copying a `Circle` into a plain `Shape` variable copies only the Shape part, called **object slicing**, and its virtual calls then go to `Shape`. Keep such objects in containers as `std::unique_ptr<Base>`.
- Don't call virtual functions from constructors or destructors expecting derived behaviour; while being built, the object is still only a base.

Each such object carries a hidden pointer to its class's **vtable**, a table of its virtual functions, and a virtual call jumps through it. That's slightly slower and stops the compiler inlining the call, which can matter in loops that run millions of times.

Use inheritance for "is-a" relationships that need polymorphism. To reuse code, prefer making the other class a data member over inheriting from it.
takeaways: `virtual` + `override` picks the function by the object's real type; always write `override`
Base classes used through pointers need a virtual destructor
Use such objects through references or pointers; copying them causes object slicing
pitfalls: Storing derived objects in a `std::vector<Base>`: they are sliced down to Base. Use `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Base>>`.

quiz.q: `Shape s = Circle{2.0}; s.name();` — Shape::name is virtual and Circle overrides it. Which runs? (Assume Shape is not abstract.)
options: Shape::name, because s is a sliced Shape object
quiz.explain: Assigning to a Shape value copies only the base part, so s really is a Shape and calls Shape::name.

quiz.q: Why does the base class need `virtual ~Shape()` when shapes are held as `std::unique_ptr<Shape>`?
options: Without it, deleting a Circle through a Shape* is undefined behaviour
unique_ptr requires every class to have a virtual destructor
It's only needed if Circle has a destructor
quiz.explain: unique_ptr<Shape> deletes through Shape*, which only calls the derived destructor correctly if the base destructor is virtual.

concepts.name: Operator overloading
concepts.summary: Give your types natural notation: arithmetic, comparisons with C++20's spaceship operator, and printing with <<.
concepts.why: Well-chosen operators make types like money, points or dates read like built-in numbers, and the standard library relies on them.
concepts.body:
You can define what operators mean for your own types by writing functions named `operator+`, `operator==`, `operator<<` and so on. The rule is to keep the usual meaning: `+` should add, `==` should compare, and nothing should surprise the reader.

Some conventions:

- Implement compound assignment (`+=`) as a member returning `*this` by reference, then write `+` in terms of it.
- Make operators with two operands, like `+` and `==`, non-members, so automatic conversions apply to both sides equally. A popular way is a **friend function** defined inside the class body (a "hidden friend"): `friend` lets a non-member use private members, and the compiler only finds it when one of the operands is your type.
- Printing with `<<` is always a non-member: `std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const T& v)`, returning `os` so calls chain.
- Other common ones: `operator[]` for indexing (C++23 allows several arguments), `operator()` to make objects you can call like functions, and `operator bool` (declare it `explicit`).

C++20 transformed comparisons. Declare `auto operator<=>(const T&) const = default;` (the **three-way comparison** or "spaceship" operator, which answers less, equal or greater in one go) and the compiler compares members in declaration order and gives you `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. A defaulted `<=>` also implicitly declares a defaulted `operator==`, so you get `==` and `!=` too. If you write `<=>` by hand, also define `==` yourself, since equality is often cheaper to compute than ordering. The result is a `std::strong_ordering` (or `partial_ordering` for doubles, where some values such as NaN can't be ordered), from `<compare>`.

The compiler also rewrites expressions: `a != b` uses `operator==`, and `b < a` can be served by `a <=> b`. That removes the old chore of writing six comparison operators by hand.

Don't overload `&&`, `||` or `,`: overloaded versions lose short-circuit evaluation and the left-to-right order.
takeaways: Keep the conventional meaning of each operator
Write `+=` as a member, `+` (and `<<`) as a non-member or hidden friend
C++20: a defaulted `<=>` gives all six comparisons
pitfalls: Writing a custom `operator<=>` and expecting `==` to appear — only a *defaulted* `<=>` declares `==` for you.

quiz.q: A struct declares only `auto operator<=>(const P&) const = default;`. Which expressions compile?
