quiz.explain: A defaulted <=> also implicitly declares a defaulted ==, and != is rewritten in terms of ==.

quiz.q: Why is `operator<<` for printing written as a non-member?
options: Its left operand is the std::ostream, which isn't your class
quiz.explain: A member operator always has the class object as its left operand, but in `std::cout << x` the left operand is the stream.

concepts.name: Scoped enums (enum class)
concepts.summary: Define named sets of constants with enum class, which are scoped, strongly typed and can choose how they are stored.
concepts.why: Enums replace unexplained numbers and true/false arguments; enum class does it without the name clashes and silent conversions of old enums.
concepts.body:
An **enum** (enumeration) is a type with a fixed set of named values, like the days of the week or the levels of a log message. C++ has two kinds.

The old C-style `enum Color { Red, Green };` puts `Red` and `Green` directly into the surrounding scope (so two enums can't both have a `None`) and converts silently to `int`, so `Red + 3` and `if (color == 1)` compile.

The C++11 **scoped enum**, `enum class Level { Debug, Info, Warn, Error };`, fixes both problems:

- Values are scoped: you write `Level::Warn`.
- No automatic conversion to integers; write a cast (an explicit conversion), `static_cast<int>(l)`, when you need the number, or C++23's `std::to_underlying(l)`.
- Values of the same enum still compare: `l >= Level::Warn`.

Behind the names, each value is stored as a whole number of an **underlying type**, `int` unless you choose another: `enum class Level : std::uint8_t` makes each value one byte, which matters in files and network messages with a fixed layout. Values count up from 0 unless you set them (`Error = 40`). An enum with a chosen underlying type can be declared before its values are listed.

`switch` on an enum is the natural way to handle each value. If the switch has no `default`, `-Wall` warns when you forget one, a useful safety net when someone adds a new value later. C++20's `using enum Level;` brings the names into scope so you can write `case Warn:` instead of `case Level::Warn:`.

Use enum class for states, modes and options instead of `int` codes or several `bool` arguments: `open(path, Mode::ReadOnly)` reads far better than `open(path, true, false)`. There's still no built-in way to turn an enum value into text; write a function with a switch.
takeaways: Prefer `enum class`: scoped names, no automatic int conversion
Choose the underlying type with `: std::uint8_t` when size matters
Switch without `default` so the compiler flags any value you forgot
pitfalls: Adding a `default:` to every enum switch, which silences the warning that would tell you about a newly added value.

quiz.q: Given `enum class Dir { Up, Down };`, which line compiles?
quiz.explain: Scoped enum values compare with each other, but don't convert to or from int and need the Dir:: prefix.

quiz.q: Why might you write `enum class Opcode : std::uint8_t`?
options: To make each Opcode exactly one byte, e.g. in a packed message
To allow implicit conversion to uint8_t
To make the values start at 1
It is required for switch statements
quiz.explain: The underlying type fixes how many bytes each value takes; conversions still need an explicit cast.

concepts.name: Standard containers
concepts.summary: Choose between vector, deque, map, set, unordered_map and friends, and use their lookup and insertion functions correctly.
concepts.why: Picking the right container is the most common design decision in C++ code and has a big effect on speed and clarity.
concepts.body:
The standard library's containers fall into a few families:

- **Sequence**: `std::vector` (the default), `std::array` (fixed size), `std::deque` (fast adding and removing at both ends), `std::list` / `std::forward_list` (a **linked list**, a chain of separately stored elements; rarely the right choice).
- **Ordered key lookup**: `std::map<K, V>` stores **key-value pairs**, like a dictionary of words (keys) and meanings (values); `std::set<K>` stores keys alone. Both keep keys sorted in a tree structure, and going through them visits keys in order.
- **Unordered key lookup**: `std::unordered_map` and `std::unordered_set` are **hash tables**: each key is turned into a number that says where to store it, so lookup is fast but there's no order. Keys need `std::hash` and `==`.
- **Adapters**: `std::stack`, `std::queue` and `std::priority_queue` (always hands out the largest item first) wrap another container to offer a narrower set of operations.

Speed is described with **Big-O notation**. A map's lookup, insert and erase are O(log n): the time grows very slowly as the map grows (a million keys take about 20 steps). A hash table's are O(1) on average: about the same time whatever the size.

Map functions have well-known traps. `m[key]` inserts a default value (0 for numbers) if the key is missing, which is handy for counting (`++freq[word]`) but surprising for lookups, and unavailable on a const map. To look up without inserting, use `contains` (C++20), `at` (throws if missing) or `find`, which returns a position marker (an iterator; next lesson) equal to `end()` when the key is missing. `try_emplace` and `insert_or_assign` are the clear ways to insert. Go through a map with a **structured binding**, which splits each pair into two names: `for (const auto& [key, value] : m)`.

Rules of thumb: start with `vector`; use `unordered_map` for fast key lookup; use `map` when you need sorted order or range questions like "the first key at least 100" (`lower_bound`). For a small, mostly-read lookup table, a sorted vector often beats both because its elements sit side by side; C++23 offers that idea as `std::flat_map` and `std::flat_set`.

All containers free everything they hold when destroyed, and copying one copies every element.
takeaways: `vector` first; `unordered_map` for fast lookup; `map` for sorted keys
`m[k]` inserts when k is missing; use `find`, `contains` or `at` to look up
Go through maps with `for (const auto& [k, v] : m)`
pitfalls: Using `if (m[key] == 0)` to test for presence, which inserts every key you test.

quiz.q: You need to print all entries sorted by key and occasionally find all keys in a range. Which container fits best?
quiz.explain: std::map keeps keys sorted, so going through them in order and asking for a range of keys (lower_bound/upper_bound) are natural.

quiz.q: After `std::map<std::string, int> m; if (m["a"] > 0) {}`, what is m.size()?
quiz.explain: [] inserts a default entry for a missing key, so "a" is now in the map with value 0.

concepts.name: Iterators
concepts.summary: Go through any container with iterators, understand half-open ranges and iterator categories, and avoid using iterators that have become invalid.
concepts.why: Iterators connect containers to the standard algorithms (ready-made functions like sort and find), and using one that has become invalid is among the most common C++ bugs.
concepts.body:
An **iterator** is a position marker inside a container that works like a pointer: `*it` gives the element, `++it` advances to the next one. Every container has `begin()`, marking the first element, and `end()`, marking the spot **one past the last**. So ranges are **half-open**, written `[begin, end)`: the start is included, the end isn't. An empty container has `begin() == end()`, and loops test `it != end()`.

The range-based for is built on these: `for (auto x : v)` is shorthand for a loop from `begin()` to `end()`. `cbegin()` gives read-only iterators and `rbegin()`/`rend()` go in reverse.

Iterators come in **iterator categories** that decide which algorithms accept them:

- Forward: only `++` (`std::forward_list`).
- Bidirectional: `++` and `--` (`std::list`, `std::map`, `std::set`).
- Random access: also jumps, `it + n`, `it[n]`, `it2 - it1` (`std::deque`).
- Contiguous: random access with the elements side by side in memory (`std::vector`, `std::array`, `std::string`).

That's why `std::sort`, which needs jumps, works on a vector but not on a list (which has its own `sort()` member function).

The critical rule is **iterator invalidation**: operations that change a container's structure can make iterators, pointers and references into it invalid, still existing but pointing at the wrong place or at freed memory. For `std::vector`, any growth into a new block makes all of them invalid, and `erase` makes everything from the erased position onwards invalid. Containers built from separately stored elements (`list`, `map`, `set`) only lose iterators to the elements actually erased. Using an invalid iterator is undefined behaviour.

To erase while looping, carry on from the iterator that `erase` returns. Better still, C++20's `std::erase(v, value)` and `std::erase_if(v, pred)` remove all matching elements in one call.
takeaways: Ranges are half-open: `[begin(), end())`; never dereference `end()`
The iterator category decides which algorithms apply (e.g. `std::sort` needs random access)
Structural changes can make iterators invalid; continue from the one `erase` returns
pitfalls: Calling `v.erase(it)` inside a for loop and then doing `++it` on the now-invalid iterator.

quiz.q: Which container's iterators allow `it + 5`?
quiz.explain: deque iterators are random access; list and map are bidirectional and forward_list is forward-only.

quiz.q: You hold an iterator to the 2nd element of a vector and then erase the 1st element. What about your iterator?
options: Invalid: erase makes iterators at or after the erased position invalid
Still valid, pointing at the same value
Automatically moved to the new 1st element
Valid only if capacity didn't change
quiz.explain: vector::erase shifts later elements down, so iterators from the erase point onwards become invalid.

concepts.name: Lambdas
concepts.summary: Write small unnamed functions inline with lambdas: captures by value and by reference, generic lambdas, and storing them for later.
concepts.why: Lambdas are how you customise sorting and searching, react to events, and hand work to other threads in modern C++.
concepts.body:
A **lambda** is a small function without a name, written right where you need it: `[captures](params) { body }`. Behind the scenes the compiler turns it into a **function object**, an object you can call like a function. The return type is worked out for you, or given as `-> T`.

The **capture list** in square brackets says which outside variables the lambda may use:

- `[x]` copies `x` into the lambda when it's created; `[&x]` refers to the original.
- `[=]` and `[&]` capture everything the body uses, by copy or by reference. Prefer listing captures explicitly in longer code.
- Captures can create new variables: `[n = 0]`, or `[p = std::move(ptr)]` to hand a `unique_ptr` over to the lambda.
- In a member function, `[this]` lets the lambda use the object's members, and `[*this]` copies the whole object.

Captured copies are const inside the lambda unless you mark it `mutable`, which lets it keep its own changing state between calls.

Each lambda has its own unique, unnamed type, so store one with `auto`. With `auto` parameters you get a **generic lambda** that accepts arguments of any type; C++20 also lets you name the type, `[]<typename T>(T x) { ... }`. Lambdas with no captures convert to plain function pointers, which code written in C can call.

To keep different callables in one variable or container, such as a list of **callbacks** (functions you hand over to be called later, when something happens), use `std::function<int(int)>` from `<functional>`. It hides the real type behind a common one, called **type erasure**, at the cost of a possible heap allocation and a slower indirect call. When you just pass a lambda straight to a function, an `auto` parameter avoids that cost. C++23 adds `std::move_only_function` for callables that can't be copied.

The main danger: a lambda that captures by reference must not outlive the variables it captured. That goes wrong with callbacks, threads and lambdas returned from functions; capture by value there.
takeaways: `[x]` copies at creation, `[&x]` refers to the live variable
Use `mutable` to change captured copies; `[p = std::move(x)]` hands things over to the lambda
`std::function` stores any callable but costs more than `auto`/templates
pitfalls: Capturing locals by reference in a callback or thread that runs after the function has returned.

quiz.q: What does this print? `int x = 1; auto f = [x] { return x; }; x = 5; std::cout << f();`
quiz.explain: A by-value capture copies x when the lambda is created, so later changes to x are not seen.

quiz.q: Why does `[n = 0]() { return ++n; }` fail to compile?
options: Captures that create new variables must be references
By-value captures are const unless the lambda is mutable
quiz.explain: A lambda's captured copies are const by default, so changing one requires `mutable`.

concepts.name: Standard algorithms
concepts.summary: Replace hand-written loops with ready-made algorithms: std::sort, find_if, transform, accumulate and the rest of <algorithm> and <numeric>.
concepts.why: Named algorithms are clearer, well tested and often faster than hand-written loops, and experienced C++ programmers expect you to know them.
concepts.body:
An **algorithm** is a step-by-step recipe for a task such as sorting or searching. The headers `<algorithm>` and `<numeric>` hold over a hundred of them as ready-made functions that work on any iterator range, usually customised with a lambda. Knowing the common ones turns ten-line loops into one line that states its intent.

- Searching: `find`, `find_if`, `any_of`/`all_of`/`none_of`, `count_if`, and on sorted ranges `binary_search`, `lower_bound`, `equal_range`.
- Sorting: `sort` (equal elements may change order), `stable_sort` (they keep their order), `partial_sort`, `nth_element` (k-th element in O(n)), `is_sorted`.
- Transforming: `transform`, `copy_if`, `fill`, `iota`, `reverse`, `rotate`, `unique`.
- Reducing: `accumulate` and `reduce` (`<numeric>`), `min_element`, `max_element`, `minmax_element`.

A **comparator**, the function that tells `sort` whether one element goes before another, must be a **strict weak ordering**: it must say false for two equal elements. Use `<`, never `<=`, or `std::sort` can misbehave and even crash.

Algorithms never change the size of a container, since they only see iterators. `remove_if` and `unique` shift the kept elements to the front and return the new logical end; you must then call `erase` to shrink the container. This two-step pattern is the **erase-remove idiom**. For the remove case, C++20's `std::erase_if` does both steps.

Watch `accumulate`'s initial value: its type is the type of the accumulator, so `accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0)` over doubles truncates every step to `int`. Pass `0.0`.

Algorithms that write, like `transform` and `copy`, write through an iterator into the destination and assume there's room: size the destination first or use `std::back_inserter(dest)`.

Since C++17, many algorithms accept an **execution policy** such as `std::execution::par` to split the work across several CPU cores at once. The C++20 range versions in the Advanced lessons take whole containers instead of iterator pairs.
takeaways: Prefer a named algorithm to a hand-written loop: it says what you mean
`remove_if`/`unique` don't shrink the container — follow with `erase` (or use `std::erase_if`)
Comparators must be strict (`<`), and `accumulate`'s initial value sets the result type
pitfalls: Passing `0` instead of `0.0` to `std::accumulate` over doubles, silently truncating the sum.

quiz.q: v is {1, 2, 3, 2} and you call `std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 2);` without erase. What is v.size() afterwards?
quiz.explain: Algorithms can't change a container's size; remove only shuffles kept elements forward and returns the new logical end.

quiz.q: What's wrong with `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a <= b; });`?
options: <= is not a strict weak ordering, so it's undefined behaviour
quiz.explain: Comparators must return false for equal elements; <= breaks that and can make sort read past the end of the range.

concepts.name: Headers, namespaces and the ODR
concepts.summary: Split code into headers and source files, organise names with namespaces, and follow the one-definition rule.
concepts.why: Every multi-file C++ project depends on this structure, and most linker errors come from getting it wrong.
concepts.body:
C++ code is split into **headers** (`.h`/`.hpp`), which contain declarations other files need, and **source files** (`.cpp`), which contain definitions. A source file `#include`s the headers it uses; the preprocessor pastes them in textually. Each header starts with `#pragma once` (supported everywhere) or the classic `#ifndef X_H / #define X_H / #endif`, so it isn't pasted in twice. (A **translation unit** is one `.cpp` file after the preprocessor has pasted in all its headers: what the compiler actually compiles in one go.) That protection is called an **include guard**.

The **one-definition rule (ODR)**: a function or variable not marked `inline` may be defined (given its body or value) only once in the whole program. If you put `int helper() { ... }` in a header included by two `.cpp` files, the linker reports "multiple definition". `inline` here means "this may be defined in several files; they're all the same thing". Things that may live in headers, because they're marked `inline` or count as inline automatically, are class definitions, templates (an Advanced topic), `inline` functions, `constexpr` functions, member functions written inside a class body, and C++17 `inline` variables. Their definitions must be identical everywhere; breaking that is undefined behaviour that no tool reports.

**Namespaces** group names and prevent clashes: `namespace geo { ... }`, used as `geo::distance`. C++17 lets you write nested ones as `namespace app::net { }`. Never write `using namespace` in a header, because it leaks into every file that includes it. In a `.cpp` file, a targeted `using std::string;` is fine.

**Linkage** decides whether a name can be seen from other files. An **unnamed namespace**, `namespace { ... }`, gives its contents internal linkage: visible only inside that `.cpp`. Use it for file-local helpers (the modern replacement for `static` functions).

C++20 **modules** (`export module geo;` / `import geo;`) and C++23's `import std;` aim to replace headers: a module is compiled once and imported, instead of being pasted as text into every file, which is faster and avoids clashes. Compiler and build-tool support is improving, but headers remain the norm.
takeaways: Headers declare, source files define; guard every header with `#pragma once`
Only inline things (classes, templates, `inline`/`constexpr` functions) may be defined in headers
Use an unnamed namespace for file-local helpers; never `using namespace` in a header
pitfalls: Defining a normal function in a header and getting "multiple definition" link errors once two files include it.

quiz.q: `int counter = 0;` is placed in a header included by a.cpp and b.cpp. What happens?
options: Each file gets its own counter
Compile error in the second file
It works; the compiler merges them
The linker reports a multiple-definition error
quiz.explain: It's a definition, not marked inline and visible from other files, that ends up in two translation units, which breaks the ODR; `inline int counter = 0;` would fix it.

quiz.q: What does wrapping a helper function in `namespace { }` in a .cpp file do?
options: Puts it in the global namespace
Makes it visible only within that translation unit
Makes it usable before its declaration
quiz.explain: Names in an unnamed namespace have internal linkage, so other files can't see or clash with them.

concepts.name: Exceptions
concepts.summary: Report errors with throw, handle them with try/catch, and rely on RAII and noexcept so errors never leave things half-done.
concepts.why: Exceptions are the standard library's error mechanism, so you need to handle them even if your own code reports errors differently.
concepts.body:
`throw` signals an error that the current function can't handle. Control leaves the function, and the functions that called it, until it reaches a matching `catch`; this **exception handling** lets the error surface where someone can deal with it. On the way out, every fully constructed local object is destroyed, which is called **stack unwinding**. That's why RAII matters: destructors free memory, close files and release locks during unwinding, so you don't need cleanup code at each exit.

Throw objects derived from `std::exception` (header `<stdexcept>` has `std::runtime_error`, `std::invalid_argument`, `std::out_of_range` and others), and **catch by const reference**: `catch (const std::exception& e)`. Catching by value copies the exception and, through object slicing, loses the derived part. Handlers are tried in order, so put specific types first. `catch (...)` catches anything; inside a handler, `throw;` rethrows the current exception.

If no handler is found, `std::terminate` ends the program.

`noexcept` declares that a function won't throw; if it does, the program terminates. Destructors are `noexcept` by default. This matters for move operations too (see Move semantics): `std::vector` only uses them while growing if they are `noexcept`.

Think about **exception-safety guarantees**, the promises a function makes about the state it leaves if an exception passes through:

- Basic: after an exception nothing leaks and objects are still valid.
- Strong: the operation either succeeds completely or has no effect at all.
- Nothrow: the operation never fails.

On mainstream compilers exceptions cost nothing while nothing is thrown, but throwing is slow (microseconds). Use them for rare failures such as a missing settings file or running out of memory, not for everyday outcomes like "key not found". Some projects (games, software for small devices) switch them off, which is why the Advanced lessons cover `std::optional` and `std::expected`.
takeaways: Throw `std::exception`-derived types; catch by `const&`, most specific first
Stack unwinding runs destructors, so RAII makes code exception-safe
Use exceptions for rare failures, not everyday outcomes
pitfalls: Catching `std::exception` before `std::out_of_range`, so the specific handler is never reached.

quiz.q: Which handler order is correct when you want to treat std::out_of_range specially and all other standard exceptions generally?
options: catch (const std::exception&) first, then catch (const std::out_of_range&)
catch (const std::out_of_range&) first, then catch (const std::exception&)
Only one catch is allowed per try
quiz.explain: Handlers are tried in order, and std::exception also matches out_of_range, so the specific one must come first.

quiz.q: A function throws while a std::vector, a std::unique_ptr and an open std::ofstream are local variables. What happens to them?
options: Their destructors run during stack unwinding, freeing memory and closing the file
They leak unless caught in the same function
Only the unique_ptr is cleaned up
quiz.explain: Stack unwinding destroys every fully constructed local, and these RAII types give back their resources in their destructors.

concepts.name: Building with CMake
concepts.summary: Describe a project with targets in CMakeLists.txt, set the C++ standard and warnings, link libraries and run tests.
concepts.why: CMake is the build system most C++ projects use; nearly every library and code editor understands it.
concepts.body:
Compiling by hand stops scaling after a few files. **CMake** doesn't compile anything itself: you describe your project once in `CMakeLists.txt`, and CMake writes the detailed instructions for a lower-level build tool such as Ninja, Make or Visual Studio. Code editors and **IDEs** (all-in-one programming apps such as CLion, VS Code or Visual Studio) open CMake projects directly.

Modern CMake is all about **CMake targets**, the things the build produces: programs and libraries.

- `add_executable(app main.cpp)` and `add_library(core STATIC a.cpp b.cpp)` define targets.
- `target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core)` links them, and also passes on core's public settings, such as the folders where its headers live (include paths) and its compiler flags.
- `target_include_directories`, `target_compile_options` and `target_compile_definitions` attach settings to one target.

The words `PRIVATE`, `PUBLIC` and `INTERFACE` matter. `PRIVATE` applies only to this target, `PUBLIC` applies to it and everything that links to it, and `INTERFACE` applies only to dependents. Avoid the old global commands like `include_directories()` and `add_compile_options()` in new code.

Set the standard with `set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)`, `CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON` and `CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF` (so you get `-std=c++20`, not `-std=gnu++20`). `CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS` writes `compile_commands.json`, a list of exact compile commands that editor helpers (clangd) and checkers (clang-tidy) read.

**Dependencies**, other people's libraries your project uses, come in through `find_package(Foo CONFIG REQUIRED)` for ones already installed (often with a C++ **package manager** such as vcpkg or Conan), or through `FetchContent`, which downloads and builds a dependency as part of your project.

Always do an **out-of-source build**: `cmake -S . -B build` puts all generated files in a separate `build` folder, away from your source code; `cmake --build build` compiles only what changed, and `ctest` runs tests registered with `add_test`. Choose `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug` (for debugging) or `Release` (optimised); multi-configuration setups such as Visual Studio pick this at build time instead. CMake presets (`CMakePresets.json`) let a team share these settings.
concepts.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(inventory LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)        # compile_commands.json for tools

add_library(core STATIC src/inventory.cpp src/storage.cpp)
target_include_directories(core PUBLIC include)   # users of core see include/
if(MSVC)
  target_compile_options(core PRIVATE /W4)
else()
  target_compile_options(core PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)
endif()

find_package(fmt CONFIG REQUIRED)            # an installed dependency
add_executable(app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core fmt::fmt)

enable_testing()
add_executable(core_tests tests/core_tests.cpp)
target_link_libraries(core_tests PRIVATE core)
add_test(NAME core_tests COMMAND core_tests)

# cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
# cmake --build build -j
# ctest --test-dir build
takeaways: Think in targets: `add_library`/`add_executable` + `target_*` commands
`PRIVATE` / `PUBLIC` / `INTERFACE` control what propagates to dependents
Configure out of source: `cmake -S . -B build`, then `cmake --build build`
pitfalls: Using global `include_directories()` and raw `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS` edits instead of per-target settings.

quiz.q: Library `core` has `target_include_directories(core PUBLIC include)`. App links core with `target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core)`. Can app's sources include headers from core's include/ directory?
options: Only if app also calls include_directories
Yes, because core declared that include directory PUBLIC
quiz.explain: PUBLIC usage requirements propagate to anything that links the target; app's PRIVATE only stops it propagating further.

quiz.q: Why set CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF?
options: So the compiler uses standard -std=c++20 instead of the GNU dialect -std=gnu++20
quiz.explain: With extensions on, GCC and Clang get -std=gnu++20, which accepts non-standard extensions.

concepts.name: Move semantics and rvalue references
concepts.summary: Transfer resources instead of copying them: rvalue references, std::move, move constructors and copy elision.
concepts.why: Move semantics is why returning big objects by value is cheap in modern C++, and you need it to write efficient resource-owning types.
concepts.body:
Copying a `std::vector` duplicates all its elements. But if the source is about to be destroyed anyway, such as a temporary or a local being returned, we could just take over its **buffer**, the block of heap memory holding the elements, instead of copying them. **Move semantics** does exactly that.

Every expression has a value category. An **lvalue** has a name and a lasting address (`x`, `v[0]`); an **rvalue** is a temporary (`f()`, `a + b`, `Buffer(8)`). An **rvalue reference**, `T&&`, binds only to rvalues. So two overloads (functions sharing a name, picked by argument type) can tell "copy from something that stays alive" from "take from something that's going away":

- `T(const T&)` is the **copy constructor**; `T(T&&)` is the **move constructor**, which takes the resource and leaves the source empty but valid.
- The same pair exists for assignment operators.

`std::move(x)` doesn't move anything. It's a cast to `T&&` that says "I'm done with `x`, you may steal from it". After a move, the object is in a **moved-from state**, valid but unspecified: you may destroy it or assign a new value, but don't rely on its contents. (Standard containers do document that a moved-from vector is empty.)

Rules that matter:

- Mark move operations `noexcept`, or `std::vector` will copy instead of move when it grows.
- Return locals by plain `return x;`. The compiler then usually builds the object directly in the caller's variable, skipping the copy entirely; this is **copy elision** (for a named local, NRVO, "named return value optimization"). If it can't, it moves automatically. Writing `return std::move(x);` can block the elision.
- Since C++17, returning or initializing from a pure temporary (a "prvalue", like `return Buffer(1024);`) is guaranteed to build in place, with no copy or move at all.
- Moving a `const` object silently copies, because `const T&&` can't bind to the move constructor.

For functions that store their argument, a common idiom is to take it by value and move it in: `void set(std::string s) { name_ = std::move(s); }`.
takeaways: `std::move` is only a cast; the move constructor does the stealing
Moved-from objects are valid but unspecified: assign or destroy them only
Return locals by name; don't `return std::move(local);`
Move operations should be `noexcept`
pitfalls: Calling `std::move` on a `const` object and getting a silent copy.

quiz.q: What does `std::move(x)` do by itself?
options: Moves x's contents into a temporary
Casts x to an rvalue reference so a move overload can be chosen
Sets x to its default value
quiz.explain: std::move is just a cast to T&&; nothing moves until a move constructor or move assignment uses it.

quiz.q: Why is `return std::move(local);` usually worse than `return local;`?
options: It can prevent copy elision (NRVO), forcing a move
It leaves local in an invalid state
quiz.explain: Returning a named local is already elided or moved automatically; the explicit cast turns the elision off.

concepts.name: Rule of zero, three and five
concepts.summary: Decide which special member functions a class needs, prefer letting members manage resources, and use =default and =delete.
concepts.why: Getting the special members wrong causes double frees, leaks and silent slow copies; these rules make it systematic.
concepts.body:
The compiler can write five **special member functions** for you, besides the default constructor: the destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor and move assignment. Which ones it writes depends on what you declare yourself.

**Rule of five** ("rule of three" before C++11 added moves). If a class needs a custom destructor, it almost certainly owns a resource directly, say through a raw pointer, so the generated copy operations, which copy the pointer and not what it points to, would be wrong: two objects would delete the same memory. Define or delete all five together. Declaring any of the destructor or copy operations suppresses the implicit move operations, so a class that only adds a destructor quietly becomes copy-only.

**Rule of zero.** Better still: don't own resources directly. Make every member manage itself, such as `std::string`, `std::vector`, `std::unique_ptr` or a small RAII wrapper, and declare none of the five. The generated versions then do the right thing member by member, and the class is copyable or move-only exactly when its members are. Most classes in good C++ code follow the rule of zero.

Write the full five only for a class whose job *is* to manage one resource, like a buffer or a handle wrapper. Tools that help:

- `= default` asks for the generated version explicitly.
- `= delete` forbids an operation: `T(const T&) = delete;` makes a type non-copyable.
- **Copy-and-swap**: take the assignment parameter by value and swap contents with it. One operator covers both copy and move assignment, and if making the copy throws an exception, the target is left untouched.
- `std::exchange(o.p_, nullptr)` reads the source pointer and nulls it in one step in move constructors.

A base class used through pointers declares `virtual ~Base() = default;` (see Inheritance), which also suppresses moves, so default them explicitly if its derived classes need to be movable.
takeaways: Rule of zero: compose RAII members and declare no special members
Rule of five: a custom destructor means you must handle copy and move too
Declaring a destructor or copy operation suppresses implicit moves
pitfalls: Adding an empty `~T() {}` "to set a breakpoint in" and silently turning every move of T into a copy.

quiz.q: A class holds `std::vector<int>` and `std::unique_ptr<Foo>` and declares no special members. What can you do with it?
options: Copy it but not move it
Move it but not copy it
quiz.explain: The generated copy constructor is deleted because unique_ptr is non-copyable, while moves are generated member-wise.

quiz.q: A class declares only a destructor `~T();`. What happens to `T b = std::move(a);`?
options: It copies, because the implicit move constructor isn't declared
quiz.explain: Declaring a destructor yourself stops the compiler writing the move operations, so the rvalue goes to the copy constructor instead.

concepts.name: Templates
concepts.summary: Write one piece of code for many types with function and class templates, deduction, non-type parameters, CTAD and variadic templates.
concepts.why: Templates power the whole standard library; reading and writing them is essential for any serious C++ work.
concepts.body:
Overloading means writing the same function again for each type. A **template** is a pattern the compiler fills in for you instead, which is C++'s form of **generics**. `template <typename T> T max_of(T a, T b)` works for any type `T` that supports `<`; calling `max_of(3, 7)` makes the compiler **instantiate** (generate) `max_of<int>`. This happens at **compile time**, while the program is being built, so it costs nothing when the program runs: each instantiation is ordinary, fully optimised code.

- **Function templates** usually work out (deduce) their type arguments from the call. Deduction needs consistent types, so `max_of(2, 2.5)` fails (is `T` int or double?); write `max_of<double>(2, 2.5)`.
- **Class templates** like `std::vector<T>` make a whole type from a pattern. Since C++17, **CTAD** (class template argument deduction) works the type out from the constructor's arguments: `std::vector v{1, 2, 3};` and `std::pair p{1, 2.5};`. C++20 extends CTAD to aggregate types.
- **Non-type template parameters** pass values known at compile time, such as sizes: `template <typename T, std::size_t N> class Ring`. C++20 allows floating-point and simple class types here as well.
- **Variadic templates** take any number of arguments, `template <typename... Ts>`, and **fold expressions** combine them all with one operator: `(xs + ... + 0)` adds them up.

Because the compiler needs the full definition to instantiate it, template code normally lives entirely in headers.

A template parameter written `T&&` in a deduced context is a **forwarding reference**, not an rvalue reference. It binds to anything, and `std::forward<T>(arg)` passes the argument on as an lvalue or rvalue, exactly as it came in. That's how `emplace_back` and `make_unique` pass constructor arguments through.

You can **specialize** a template, giving it a separate version for particular arguments, `template <> struct Hash<MyType> { ... };`, to give a custom implementation.

The traditional downside is error messages: a type that lacks an operation fails deep inside the template's code, with pages of output. Concepts, next, fix that.
takeaways: Templates generate code for each set of arguments at compile time, at no cost when the program runs
Template definitions go in headers
In a deduced `template <class T> f(T&& x)`, `T&&` is a forwarding reference; pass it on with `std::forward<T>(x)`
pitfalls: Declaring a template in a header and defining it in a .cpp file, then getting undefined-reference link errors.

quiz.q: Why does `max_of(2, 2.5)` fail for `template <typename T> T max_of(T a, T b)`?
options: Deduction gets int from one argument and double from the other, a conflict
quiz.explain: Each argument deduces T independently; int and double disagree, so deduction fails.

quiz.q: In `template <typename T> void wrap(T&& arg)`, what is `T&&`?
options: A forwarding reference that binds to lvalues and rvalues
quiz.explain: When T is deduced, T&& is a forwarding reference: T becomes U& for lvalues, so it binds to everything.

concepts.name: Concepts and constraints
concepts.summary: Constrain templates with C++20 concepts and requires clauses for clear errors and overloading by capability.
concepts.why: Concepts turn template errors from pages of noise into one line and document what a template actually needs.
concepts.body:
A **concept** is a named yes/no test on a type, checked at compile time. `std::integral<T>` is true for integer types; `std::totally_ordered<T>` for types with all comparisons. The header `<concepts>` provides the core set (`same_as`, `convertible_to`, `derived_from`, `invocable`, `regular`...), and `<iterator>` and `<ranges>` add many more.

Using a concept to limit which types a template accepts is called a **constraint**. You can write one in several equivalent ways:

- `template <std::integral T> T half(T x);`
- `template <typename T> requires std::integral<T> T half(T x);`
- Abbreviated: `auto half(std::integral auto x);`

If a call doesn't satisfy the constraint, the error names the failed concept at the call site instead of failing somewhere inside the template body.

Define your own with a **requires-expression**, which lists the operations a type must support:

```cpp
template <typename T>
concept Shape = requires(const T& s) {
    { s.area() } -> std::convertible_to<double>;
};
```

Each requirement must compile for the concept to hold; the `-> concept` part also checks the result type.

Constraints take part in overload resolution. You can write one `half` for integers and one for floating-point types, and the right one is picked; when one constraint includes another (for example `A && B` includes `A`), it **subsumes** it, and the more constrained overload wins. This replaces most uses of the older tricks SFINAE and `enable_if` (an Expert lesson).

Concepts are checked by structure: a type satisfies `Shape` if it has the right members, without deriving from any base class. That's **duck typing** ("if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck"), but checked at compile time with good errors.

Use the standard concepts when they fit, and design your own around meaningful ideas ("a Shape", "a Sortable range") rather than single operations.
takeaways: Constrain templates with `template <Concept T>`, `requires`, or `Concept auto`
Define concepts with requires-expressions listing the needed operations
Constraints take part in overload resolution and replace most older template tricks
pitfalls: Writing a concept for a single operation ("HasPlus") instead of a meaningful abstraction.

quiz.q: What happens when you call `half("text")` with only the two constrained overloads above?
options: It compiles but fails at run time
Compile error: no overload's constraints are satisfied
quiz.explain: const char* is neither integral nor floating point, so both candidates are removed and no viable function remains.

quiz.q: A type `Circle` has `double area() const` and `std::string name() const` but no base class. Does it satisfy the Shape concept above?
options: No, it must derive from Shape
Yes, concepts check the required expressions structurally
quiz.explain: Concept satisfaction is checked by whether the requirements compile; no inheritance or registration is involved.

concepts.name: Ranges and views
concepts.summary: Use C++20 ranges: algorithms on whole containers with projections, and lazy views chained together with |.
concepts.why: Ranges make multi-step data processing shorter and safer than pairs of iterators, and views avoid building temporary containers.
concepts.body:
C++20's `<ranges>` brings two big improvements.

A **range** is anything with a `begin()` and an `end()`, such as any container. **Range algorithms**: everything in `std::ranges::` accepts a whole range: `std::ranges::sort(v)` instead of `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end())`. They're constrained with concepts, so misuse produces readable errors, and they accept a **projection**, a function applied to each element before comparing. `std::ranges::sort(staff, {}, &Employee::age)` sorts by age with no lambda; `std::ranges::find(staff, "Mo", &Employee::name)` finds by name.

**Range views.** A view is a lightweight range that doesn't own elements: it works them out on demand from another range, which is **lazy evaluation**. Chain views with `|` into a **pipeline**, where each step's output feeds the next:

- `views::filter(pred)`, `views::transform(f)`, `views::take(n)`, `views::drop(n)`, `views::reverse`
- `views::iota(a, b)` generates numbers; `views::iota(1)` counts forever (fine when combined with `take`)
- `views::keys` / `views::values` on maps, `views::split`, `views::join`

Nothing runs until you iterate, and each element flows through the whole pipeline individually, with no intermediate vectors. C++23 adds `views::zip`, `views::enumerate`, `views::chunk`, `views::slide`, and `std::ranges::to<std::vector>()` to collect a view into a container.

Things to watch:

- Views refer to their underlying data. A view over a container must not outlive it, just like an iterator.
- Some views (such as `filter`) remember their first position after computing it once, so they must be non-const to loop over; pass views to functions by value or forwarding reference rather than `const&`.
- Range algorithms called on a temporary container return the placeholder `std::ranges::dangling` instead of an iterator, so the compiler stops you from using a result that would point into a destroyed container.
takeaways: `std::ranges::` algorithms take whole ranges and support projections
Views are lazy and non-owning; compose them with `|`
A view must not outlive the data it looks at
pitfalls: Returning a view over a local container from a function — the view dangles once the container is destroyed.

quiz.q: When does the filter lambda in `auto v = nums | std::views::filter(pred);` run?
options: When v is copied into a vector automatically
quiz.explain: Views are lazy: elements are filtered on demand as the iteration reaches them.

quiz.q: What does `std::ranges::sort(people, {}, &Person::height)` do?
options: Sorts people by height using the default less-than comparator
Sorts heights into a new vector
Doesn't compile: the comparator can't be {}
quiz.explain: {} picks the default comparison (less than), and the projection makes it compare the height members while sorting the Person objects.

concepts.name: constexpr and compile-time code
concepts.summary: Run code at compile time with constexpr, consteval and constinit, and check assumptions with static_assert.
concepts.why: Moving work and checks to compile time catches bugs earlier and removes runtime cost, and modern C++ lets you do it with normal code.
concepts.body:
A `constexpr` function can be evaluated by the compiler when its arguments are constants, and is an ordinary function otherwise. Modern `constexpr` functions may use loops, local variables, `if` and `switch`, and since C++20 even virtual calls, `try` blocks, and a `std::vector` or `std::string` that is created and destroyed during the calculation.

- `constexpr` variables must be given a **constant expression**, a value the compiler can work out, and are automatically `const`. They can size arrays, be template arguments and be used in `static_assert`.
- `static_assert(cond, "msg")` fails the build if `cond` is false, documenting assumptions about sizes, layouts and constants.
- C++20 `consteval` makes an **immediate function**: every call must be worked out at compile time. Use it when a call at run time would be a mistake, such as checking format strings.
- C++20 `constinit` guarantees a global variable gets its value at compile time while staying changeable. That avoids a classic bug: globals in different files set up at run time in an unpredictable order, one reading another before it's ready.
- `if constexpr (cond)` discards the untaken branch at compile time inside templates, so it doesn't even need to compile for that type.

A nice trick is building lookup tables with a lambda (a small unnamed function written inline) that is called on the spot: `constexpr auto table = [] { ... return t; }();`. The compiler computes the table and stores it inside the executable.

A huge benefit: undefined behaviour isn't allowed in constant evaluation. Overflow, out-of-bounds access and use of uninitialized values become compile errors, so `static_assert` tests of constexpr functions double as UB checks.

`std::is_constant_evaluated()` (C++20) and C++23's `if consteval` let a function choose a different implementation at compile time, for example avoiding special CPU instructions that the compiler can't run itself.

Compile-time work isn't free: it costs build time, and compilers cap how many steps they'll evaluate. Use it for tables, validation and configuration, not big computations.
takeaways: `constexpr` functions run at compile time when given constants, at run time otherwise
`consteval` forces compile time; `constinit` forces a global's starting value to be set at compile time
UB is a compile error in constant evaluation, so `static_assert` tests catch it
pitfalls: Assuming a `constexpr` function call is always computed at compile time — only contexts that require a constant guarantee it.

quiz.q: `constexpr int sq(int x) { return x * x; }` is called as `sq(n)` where n is read from std::cin. What happens?
options: Compile error: n is not a constant
The compiler reads n at build time
It runs at run time like a normal function
quiz.explain: constexpr allows compile-time evaluation but doesn't require it; with a runtime argument it is an ordinary call.

quiz.q: Which keyword makes every call of a function a compile-time evaluation?
quiz.explain: consteval declares an immediate function; a call that can't be evaluated at compile time is an error.

concepts.name: optional, variant and expected
concepts.summary: Model maybe-values with std::optional, one-of-several types with std::variant and std::visit, and errors as values with C++23 std::expected.
concepts.why: These standard building-block types replace sentinel values (special values like -1 meaning "not found"), null pointers and many exceptions with types the compiler checks.
concepts.body:
**`std::optional<T>`** (C++17) holds either a `T` or nothing. It's the clear return type for "might not have a result": `std::optional<int> parse_int(std::string_view)`. Test it with `if (opt)` or `has_value()`, read it with `*opt` (unchecked) or `opt.value()` (throws `std::bad_optional_access`), and supply a fallback with `value_or(x)`. The value is stored inline, so there's no heap allocation. C++23 adds `and_then`, `transform` and `or_else` to chain several steps that might each produce nothing.

**`std::variant<A, B, C>`** (C++17) holds exactly one of several types at a time, and remembers which one: a **tagged union**. It's also stored inline. It is an alternative to inheritance for a fixed set of types: no virtual functions, no heap, and the compiler knows every possibility.

- `std::holds_alternative<B>(v)` tests the active type, `std::get<B>(v)` reads it (throws if wrong), `std::get_if<B>(&v)` returns a pointer or null.
- `std::visit(visitor, v)` calls the visitor, a callable, with whichever type is active. With the `overloaded` helper (a struct that inherits the call operators of several lambdas) you write one lambda per type, and forgetting a type is a compile error.

**`std::expected<T, E>`** (C++23, `<expected>`) holds either a value or an error of type `E`. It reports failure without exceptions while keeping the reason:

```cpp
std::expected<Config, std::string> load(std::string_view path);
auto cfg = load("app.toml");
if (!cfg) log(cfg.error());
```

Return `std::unexpected(err)` to signal failure. It has the same chaining functions as optional.

Which to use: exceptions for rare failures far from where they're handled; `optional` when absence needs no explanation; `expected` when callers handle errors right away and need the reason; `variant` for states and messages with a fixed set of shapes.
takeaways: `optional<T>`: a value or nothing; `value_or` gives a fallback
`variant` + `std::visit`: a closed set of types, checked exhaustively
C++23 `expected<T, E>`: a value or an error, without exceptions
pitfalls: Calling `*opt` without checking — dereferencing an empty optional is undefined behaviour.

quiz.q: A lookup may find nothing, and the caller just needs to know whether it did. Which return type fits best?
quiz.explain: optional expresses "value or nothing" with no extra error information and no allocation.

quiz.q: What does std::visit with an `overloaded` set of lambdas give you over a chain of holds_alternative checks?
options: A compile error if an alternative is not handled
quiz.explain: visit must be callable for every alternative, so a missing lambda fails to compile.

concepts.name: Threads, mutexes and atomics
concepts.summary: Run work in parallel with std::jthread, protect shared data with mutexes and scoped locks, and use atomics for simple counters.
concepts.why: Today's CPUs have many cores, and two threads touching the same data without care is undefined behaviour, so correct synchronisation is a core skill.
concepts.body:
A **thread** is one line of execution inside a running program; several threads run at the same time, on different **CPU cores**, and share the same memory. Running work this way is **concurrency** (and when it truly happens at the same instant, **parallelism**).

`std::thread` starts a function on a new thread. You must `join()` it (wait for it to finish) or `detach()` it (let it run on its own) before the `std::thread` object is destroyed, or the program calls `std::terminate` and stops. C++20's **`std::jthread`** joins automatically in its destructor (RAII again) and supports polite cancellation: the thread function can take a `std::stop_token` and regularly check `stop_requested()`, and `request_stop()` asks it to finish. Prefer `jthread`.

When threads share data and at least one writes, you need synchronization. An unsynchronized read and write at the same time is a **data race**, which is undefined behaviour, not just a wrong number.

- A **mutex** (`std::mutex`, "mutual exclusion") lets only one thread at a time into a section of code. Never call `lock()`/`unlock()` by hand; use `std::scoped_lock lock{m};` (C++17), which unlocks at scope exit even when an exception passes through. `scoped_lock` can lock several mutexes at once without a **deadlock**, where two threads each wait forever for a lock the other holds. Use `std::unique_lock` when you need to unlock early or wait on a condition variable.
- A **condition variable** (`std::condition_variable`) lets a thread sleep until another one tells it that something it was waiting for (checked under the mutex) has become true.
- `std::atomic<T>` makes single operations on small values (`++`, `load`, `store`, `fetch_add`, `compare_exchange`) an **atomic operation**: indivisible, so no other thread sees it half done, and no lock needed. Good for counters and flags; for rules that span several variables, use a mutex.

Higher-level tools: `std::async` runs a function and returns a `std::future`, from which you collect the result later; C++20 adds `std::latch`, `std::barrier` and `std::counting_semaphore` for making threads wait for each other.

Practical advice: share as little as possible, hold locks briefly and never call unknown code while holding one, and pass data to threads by value. Capturing locals by reference in a thread's lambda is only safe if the thread is joined before those locals die. Test with `-fsanitize=thread`, which detects data races while the program runs.
takeaways: A data race (a write plus another access at the same time, unsynchronised) is undefined behaviour
Prefer `std::jthread`; lock with `std::scoped_lock`, never manual lock/unlock
Atomics for single counters/flags, mutexes for rules spanning several variables
pitfalls: Letting a `std::thread` object be destroyed while still joinable, which calls `std::terminate`.

quiz.q: Two threads each run `++count;` 1000 times on a plain `int count = 0;`. What is guaranteed?
options: The second thread waits for the first
Nothing: it's a data race, which is undefined behaviour
quiz.explain: Unsynchronised concurrent writes are a data race; the standard gives no guarantee at all, not even a range.

quiz.q: What advantage does std::jthread have over std::thread?
options: It joins automatically in its destructor and supports stop tokens
quiz.explain: jthread is the RAII version of thread and adds cooperative cancellation via std::stop_token.

concepts.name: Undefined behaviour
concepts.summary: Know what undefined behaviour is, the common ways to cause it, why optimisers make it dangerous, and the tools that find it.
concepts.why: UB is the source of C++'s worst bugs and of many **vulnerabilities**, weaknesses an attacker can exploit; experienced developers recognise the patterns on sight.
concepts.body:
The C++ standard, the official rulebook, sorts program behaviour into categories. **Implementation-defined** behaviour, like `sizeof(long)`, varies by platform but is documented. **Unspecified** behaviour, like the order in which a function's arguments are worked out, is one of several allowed outcomes, not documented. **Undefined behaviour (UB)** means the standard places no requirements at all: the program may crash, appear to work, or do something bizarre.

The danger is the **optimizer**, the part of the compiler that rewrites your code to run faster. It assumes UB never happens and rewrites on that assumption. If `x + 1 < x` can only be true by overflowing a signed int, the compiler may fold it to `false`. If you dereference a pointer and later check it for null, the check may be deleted. UB can also appear to "travel back in time" and affect code that ran before it.

Common sources:

- Signed integer overflow, division by zero, shifting by the type's width or more.
- Out-of-bounds access (`v[i]`, raw arrays, pointer arithmetic beyond the array).
- Null, dangling or freed pointers and references, including iterators made invalid by `push_back` and `string_view`s into destroyed strings.
- Reading an uninitialized variable. (C++26 makes this "erroneous behaviour" with defined consequences, but it's still a bug.)
- Data races: two threads (parts of a program running at the same time) using the same data without coordination, at least one of them writing.
- Breaking **strict aliasing**, the rule that you may only read an object through a pointer to its own type (reading a `float` through a `uint32_t*` breaks it), and other misuse of objects outside their lifetime.
- Changing an object created const, or a loop that runs forever without any **side effect** (no output, no change visible outside it).

Your defences: compile with `-Wall -Wextra`; test with a **sanitizer**, `-fsanitize=address,undefined` (and `thread` for races), which adds run-time checks that report UB as it happens; run **static analysis** tools like clang-tidy, which inspect source code for risky patterns without running it; use checked access (`at()`) where speed isn't critical, and the hardened (extra-checking) modes of the standard library; and prefer RAII and types that behave like plain values, which make lifetime errors hard to write. `constexpr` evaluation also rejects UB, so compile-time tests catch it.
takeaways: UB means no guarantees; the optimiser assumes it never happens
Usual suspects: overflow, out of bounds, dangling pointers/refs, uninitialised reads, data races
Sanitizers (`-fsanitize=address,undefined,thread`) and warnings find most of it
pitfalls: Concluding code is fine because it "works on my machine" — UB can change behaviour with a new compiler, flag or input.

quiz.q: `int* p = get(); int v = *p; if (p == nullptr) return;` — what may an optimising compiler do?
options: Move the null check before the dereference
Remove the null check, since p was already dereferenced and so can't be null
Insert a runtime null check automatically
quiz.explain: Dereferencing null is UB, so the compiler may assume p is non-null and delete the later check.

quiz.q: Which of these is implementation-defined rather than undefined?
options: Reading past the end of an array
quiz.explain: The size of long varies by platform but is documented; the others are undefined behaviour.

concepts.name: Memory model and atomic ordering
concepts.summary: Understand the happens-before rule, and choose between seq_cst, acquire/release and relaxed memory orders for atomics.
concepts.why: Code that coordinates threads without locks depends on memory ordering; getting it wrong produces bugs that appear only on some CPUs and some days.
concepts.body:
To go faster, compilers and CPUs reorder reads and writes of memory freely, as long as a single thread can't tell. Other threads can. The C++ **memory model** defines what one thread is guaranteed to see of another's writes. Its core is the **happens-before** relation: if A happens-before B, everything A wrote is visible to B. A program without data races behaves as if operations were interleaved in an order consistent with happens-before; a program with a data race has undefined behaviour.

Atomic operations take a **memory order**, `std::memory_order`, saying how much ordering they enforce:

- `seq_cst` (the default): all seq_cst operations appear in one global order that every thread agrees on. The easiest to reason about, and a bit more expensive on CPU families that reorder a lot (ARM, POWER) and for stores on x86 (the Intel/AMD family).
- `release` (on stores) and `acquire` (on loads): if an acquire load reads the value written by a release store, everything the writer did before the store **happens-before** everything the reader does after the load. This "publish data, then raise a flag" pattern is what mutexes, thread-safe queues and one-time setup are built on.
- `relaxed`: the operation itself is atomic, but there are no ordering guarantees for other memory. Fine for statistics counters and for compare-and-swap loops (below) where only the atomic value matters.
- `acq_rel` for read-modify-write operations that both acquire and release. (`consume` exists but compilers treat it as `acquire`, and it's being removed.)

x86 CPUs reorder little, so a missing acquire/release often only shows up on ARM (most phones, Apple Silicon Macs), which is a good reason to rely on the model rather than on testing.

**Compare-and-swap** (`compare_exchange_weak(expected, desired)`) stores `desired` only if the value still equals `expected`, in one atomic step. It is the building block of **lock-free** algorithms, which coordinate threads without any mutex. On failure it loads the current value into `expected`, so it belongs in a loop; the weak form may also fail for no reason, but is cheaper on CPUs such as ARM. C++20 also adds `atomic::wait`/`notify_one`, which let a thread sleep until a value changes, and `std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>`.

Start with mutexes or seq_cst; weaken orderings only with a proof and a benchmark (a careful speed measurement).
takeaways: A release store read by an acquire load makes all prior writes visible
`relaxed` = atomicity only; fine for counters, wrong for publishing data
Default `seq_cst` is easiest; weaken only with proof and measurements
pitfalls: Publishing data with a relaxed flag: it may work on x86 and fail on ARM.

quiz.q: In the producer/consumer above, both orders are changed to memory_order_relaxed. What is the consequence?
options: The consumer may see ready == true but read a stale payload — a data race on payload
quiz.explain: Relaxed operations create no happens-before edge, so the payload write isn't guaranteed to be visible and the access races.

quiz.q: Why is compare_exchange_weak normally called in a loop?
options: It only works on every second call
It may fail spuriously and, on failure, updates expected with the current value to retry with
It blocks until the value changes
quiz.explain: The weak form can fail even when the values match, and the refreshed expected value lets the loop retry correctly.

concepts.name: Template metaprogramming and SFINAE
concepts.summary: Compute with types at compile time: type traits, SFINAE and enable_if, the detection idiom, if constexpr, and how concepts replace them.
concepts.why: Library code and older codebases are full of these techniques, and they explain how the standard library makes compile-time decisions.
concepts.body:
**Template metaprogramming** uses templates to compute with types and constants at compile time. The standard toolkit lives in `<type_traits>`, a collection of **type traits**, small templates that answer a question about a type or transform it: predicates like `std::is_integral_v<T>`, `std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>` and `std::is_base_of_v<B, D>`; transformations like `std::remove_cvref_t<T>`, `std::decay_t<T>` and `std::conditional_t<cond, A, B>`; and `std::integral_constant` / `std::bool_constant` as base classes for writing your own traits.

**SFINAE**, "substitution failure is not an error", is the rule that makes the old techniques work. While the compiler plugs template arguments into a candidate function's *signature* (its parameter and return types), an invalid type or expression just removes that candidate from overload resolution instead of causing an error. Errors inside the function *body* are still hard errors.

- `std::enable_if_t<cond, int> = 0` as a template parameter enables an overload only when `cond` holds.
- The **detection idiom** asks "does this expression compile for T?". It uses a partial specialization (a template specialization for a family of arguments) with `std::void_t<decltype(expr)>`: if the expression is valid, the specialization deriving from `std::true_type` is chosen, otherwise the general one deriving from `std::false_type`.
- `decltype(expr)` gives the type of an expression, and `std::declval<T>()` pretends to produce a `T`, so you can form expressions on types without creating objects.

C++17 `if constexpr` removed much of the need for overload tricks: the discarded branch isn't instantiated, so it may contain code that wouldn't compile for that `T`. Fold expressions replaced most recursive variadic templates.

C++20 concepts replace the rest. `template <std::integral T>` says what `enable_if` used to say, with better errors and proper subsumption, and a requires-expression is the detection idiom built into the language. Write new code with concepts and `if constexpr`; learn SFINAE to read and maintain existing libraries, and for the rare situations where you still need a trait class.
takeaways: SFINAE: invalid substitution in a signature removes the candidate silently
`<type_traits>` + `decltype`/`declval` are the metaprogramming toolkit
Prefer concepts and `if constexpr` in new code
pitfalls: Expecting SFINAE to apply to errors inside a function body — only the immediate signature context is SFINAE-friendly.

quiz.q: What does SFINAE do when substituting T into a candidate's return type produces an invalid type?
options: Removes that candidate from the overload set and keeps looking
Delays the error until run time
quiz.explain: Substitution failure in the immediate context isn't an error; the candidate is just not viable.

quiz.q: Why does `if constexpr (has_size<T>::value) return x.size(); else return sizeof(T);` compile for T = int?
options: The discarded branch inside a template is not instantiated
int has a hidden size() member
if constexpr converts errors into false
sizeof makes the whole function constexpr
quiz.explain: In a template, the branch not taken by if constexpr is discarded, so x.size() is never checked for int.

concepts.name: Object lifetime and layout
concepts.summary: How objects occupy memory: storage versus lifetime, construct_at and destroy_at, alignment and padding, trivially copyable types and bit_cast.
concepts.why: Containers, custom memory management, saving objects as bytes, and low-level optimisation all depend on the exact rules for when an object exists and how it's laid out.
concepts.body:
In C++, storage (the bytes) and **object lifetime** (the time during which an object exists in them) are separate. Memory can exist without an object in it, and an object's lifetime begins only when it's constructed and ends when its destructor runs (or its storage is reused). Accessing an object outside its lifetime is undefined behaviour, even if the bytes are still there.

That's how `std::vector` works: it allocates raw capacity, then builds elements in that memory with **placement new**, `new (ptr) T(args)` ("construct a T at this address"), or C++20's `std::construct_at(ptr, args...)`, and destroys them with `std::destroy_at(ptr)` without freeing the memory. If you reuse storage in tricky ways (const members, a different type), `std::launder` may be needed to obtain a valid pointer to the new object.

**Layout.** Every type has a size and an **alignment** (`alignof`): its address must be a multiple of that number, because CPUs read aligned data fastest. Members are laid out in declaration order with **padding**, unused filler bytes, inserted so each is properly aligned, and the struct's size is padded to a multiple of its alignment. Ordering members from largest to smallest alignment often shrinks a struct, which matters for big arrays. `alignas(64)` raises alignment, for example to give a variable its own **cache line**, the 64-byte chunk in which the CPU moves memory into its cache.

Type properties decide what's legal:

- **Trivially copyable** types (no custom copy, move or destructor) may be copied byte by byte with `memcpy`.
- **Standard-layout** types are laid out the way C would lay them out, and `offsetof` (a member's distance from the start) works on them.
- **Implicit-lifetime** types (for example aggregate types made only of numbers and pointers) start to exist automatically in memory obtained from C's `malloc` or filled by `memcpy`, since C++20; C++23's `std::start_lifetime_as` does it explicitly.

To read the bits of one type as another, called **type punning**, use C++20's `std::bit_cast<To>(from)` (or `memcpy`). Reading a `float` through a `uint32_t*` breaks strict aliasing and is UB. C++20's `[[no_unique_address]]` lets an empty member take no space, which is how containers store their allocator and comparator objects for free.
takeaways: Storage and lifetime are separate: construct_at begins it, destroy_at ends it
Padding follows alignment; order members largest-first to shrink structs
Use `std::bit_cast` or `memcpy` for type punning, never pointer casts
pitfalls: Using `memcpy` on a type that isn't trivially copyable (e.g. one containing a std::string).

quiz.q: What is sizeof(S) for `struct S { char c; int i; char d; };` on a typical platform with 4-byte int alignment?
quiz.explain: c at 0, 3 bytes padding, i at 4, d at 8, then padding to a multiple of 4 gives 12.

quiz.q: Which is a well-defined way to get the bit pattern of a float as a uint32_t?
options: A union, writing f and reading the integer member
quiz.explain: bit_cast copies the object representation; the pointer cast breaks strict aliasing, static_cast converts the value, and union punning is UB in C++.

concepts.name: Linking, libraries and the ABI
concepts.summary: How the linker matches up symbols, name mangling, static versus shared libraries, ABI compatibility, extern "C" and the pimpl idiom.
concepts.why: Shipping libraries, fixing link errors and upgrading compilers safely all require understanding symbols and the ABI.
concepts.body:
Each object file has a symbol table: the names (**linker symbols**) of the functions and variables it defines and of those it needs from elsewhere. The linker matches them up. **Linkage** decides visibility: external (shared across translation units, the default for functions and global variables), internal (`static` or an unnamed namespace, private to one file) or none (locals).

Overloading and namespaces mean a plain C++ name like `area` isn't unique, so compilers encode the namespace and parameter types into the symbol, called **name mangling**: `geo::area(double)` becomes `_ZN3geo4areaEd` under the Itanium C++ ABI used on Linux and macOS (MSVC has its own scheme). `nm -C` and `c++filt` demangle. `extern "C"` turns mangling off, giving a plain C symbol; use it to call or be called from C, and for the functions a program looks up by name in a plugin.

Libraries come in two kinds. A **static library** (`.a`, `.lib`) is an archive of object files copied into the executable at link time. With GNU ld, order matters: list libraries after the objects that use them. A **shared library** (`.so`, `.dylib`, `.dll`) is a separate file loaded when the program starts and shared between running programs. That makes its **ABI** (application binary interface), the exact machine-level details that compiled code relies on, a contract.

The ABI covers the **calling convention** (where arguments and results are placed during a call), name mangling, object layout, vtable layout and how exceptions travel. Changing a public class's data members, adding a virtual function, or changing an inline function or template in a header breaks the ABI: existing binaries silently use the old layout. Even standard library types change, as with libstdc++'s `std::string` switch, controlled by `_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI`. Mixing code built against different standard libraries or with incompatible flags causes link errors or worse.

To keep a stable ABI, hide data behind the **pimpl idiom** ("pointer to implementation") (`class Widget { struct Impl; std::unique_ptr<Impl> p_; };`), so the layout lives in the `.cpp`; or offer a plain C interface. On Linux (whose binary format is called ELF), build with `-fvisibility=hidden` and export only the public symbols.
concepts.code:
# lib.cpp:  namespace geo { double area(double r) { return 3.14159 * r * r; } }
#           extern "C" double geo_area(double r) { return geo::area(r); }
g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -fPIC -c lib.cpp -o lib.o
nm lib.o
#   T _ZN3geo4areaEd        mangled C++ name (Itanium ABI)
#   T geo_area              extern "C": plain, unmangled
nm -C lib.o                 # demangled: geo::area(double)
echo _ZN3geo4areaEd | c++filt

# static library: archive of objects, copied into the executable
ar rcs libgeo.a lib.o
g++ main.o -L. -lgeo -o app            # libraries AFTER the objects that need them

# shared library: loaded at run time, its ABI is now a contract
g++ -shared -o libgeo.so lib.o
g++ main.o -L. -lgeo -Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN' -o app
ldd app | grep geo

# undefined reference to `geo::area(double)'  -> definition not linked, or wrong order
# multiple definition of `helper()'           -> non-inline function defined in a header
takeaways: C++ names are mangled into symbols; `extern "C"` gives plain C symbols
Static libraries are copied in at link time; shared libraries make the ABI a contract
Pimpl or a C API keeps a library's ABI stable across changes
pitfalls: Adding a data member or virtual function to a class exported from a shared library without rebuilding all its users.

quiz.q: A shared library adds a private data member to a public class whose definition is in its header. Existing apps aren't rebuilt. What's the risk?
options: The apps still use the old object size and layout, causing memory corruption
A compile error in the apps
The dynamic loader adapts the layout automatically
quiz.explain: Code compiled against the old header allocates and accesses objects with the old size and offsets, which is an ABI break.

quiz.q: Why is `extern "C"` used for plugin entry points like `create_plugin()`?
options: It gives an unmangled symbol name that dlsym/GetProcAddress can find reliably
It allows the function to throw exceptions across the boundary
quiz.explain: C linkage turns off name mangling, so the symbol name is predictable across compilers.

concepts.name: Allocators and polymorphic memory resources
concepts.summary: Control where containers get memory: the allocator model, std::pmr memory resources, arenas and pools.
concepts.why: Allocation is often the hidden cost in code that runs millions of times; custom memory resources can make it several times faster and more predictable.
takeaways: Containers allocate through their allocator parameter
`std::pmr` puts the strategy in a runtime memory_resource, keeping one container type
Monotonic arenas make allocation a pointer bump and free everything at once
pitfalls: Letting a memory resource be destroyed while a pmr container still uses it.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of std::pmr::vector<int> over std::vector<int, MyAlloc<int>>?
options: Vectors backed by different memory resources still have the same type
quiz.explain: The resource is chosen at run time through a pointer, so the allocator strategy isn't baked into the type.

quiz.q: Why is deallocate a no-op in monotonic_buffer_resource?
options: It hands memory back to the OS immediately
It frees everything at once when the resource is destroyed or released, which makes allocation a cheap pointer bump
Deallocation happens on a background thread
quiz.explain: A monotonic arena only grows; memory is reclaimed in bulk, trading reuse for very fast allocation.

concepts.name: Coroutines under the hood
concepts.summary: How C++20 coroutines work: the coroutine frame, promise_type, coroutine_handle, awaiters, and C++23 std::generator.
concepts.why: Coroutines power generators and libraries that wait for slow input and output (I/O) such as network traffic without blocking a thread; using them safely requires knowing what the compiler generates.
concepts.body:
A **coroutine** is a function that can pause in the middle and later carry on where it left off. In C++, a function becomes one as soon as its body uses `co_await`, `co_yield` or `co_return`. C++20 coroutines are stackless: instead of keeping their own call stack, they store the locals that must survive a pause in a heap-allocated **coroutine frame**, which the compiler may avoid allocating when the coroutine finishes within its caller's lifetime.

The language supplies the mechanism; libraries supply the types. The return type (say `Generator<int>`, a **generator** that produces a sequence of values one at a time) must contain a nested **`promise_type`**, which customises behaviour:

- `get_return_object()` builds what the caller receives, usually holding a `std::coroutine_handle<promise_type>`.
- `initial_suspend()` decides whether the body starts at once or only when first resumed; `final_suspend()` whether the frame stays alive after finishing (it must be `noexcept`).
- `yield_value(v)`, `return_value(v)`/`return_void()` and `unhandled_exception()` handle `co_yield`, `co_return` and exceptions.

A **coroutine handle**, `std::coroutine_handle`, is a non-owning pointer to the frame, with `resume()`, `done()`, `destroy()` and `promise()`. Someone must call `destroy()` exactly once, which is why wrapper types are move-only RAII classes.

`co_await expr` asks an **awaiter** object, through three functions, whether and how to pause: `await_ready()` (skip suspending?), `await_suspend(handle)` (store the handle somewhere, such as a list of operations waiting for the network, to resume later) and `await_resume()` (the result). `std::suspend_always` and `std::suspend_never` are trivial awaiters.

The biggest pitfall is lifetime. Reference parameters, and lambda captures for coroutine lambdas, are not copied into the frame, so a coroutine resumed after its caller's arguments died reads dangling memory. Take parameters by value.

C++23 adds `std::generator<T>` in `<generator>`, so you rarely write generators yourself; for async work use a library such as cppcoro, Asio or the C++26 `std::execution` model.
takeaways: Any of `co_await`/`co_yield`/`co_return` makes a coroutine with a heap frame
`promise_type` customises behaviour; `coroutine_handle` resumes and destroys
Take coroutine parameters by value; references may dangle across suspensions
pitfalls: Passing a `const std::string&` to a lazily started coroutine with a temporary argument — it dangles before the body runs.

quiz.q: With `initial_suspend()` returning std::suspend_always, when does the coroutine body start running?
options: On the first resume() of its handle
Immediately when the coroutine function is called
When the return object is destroyed
quiz.explain: Suspending initially returns control to the caller before any body code runs; the body starts at the first resume.

quiz.q: Why does the Generator wrapper call h_.destroy() in its destructor?
options: The coroutine frame is not freed automatically after final suspension; the owner must destroy it
To resume the coroutine one last time
To reset the promise's current value
quiz.explain: A coroutine that suspends at final_suspend keeps its frame alive until someone calls destroy() on its handle.

concepts.name: Performance and cache-friendly code
concepts.summary: Write fast C++: measure first, then exploit caches with contiguous data, avoid needless allocations and copies, and prevent false sharing.
concepts.why: Modern CPUs are limited by memory far more than arithmetic; data layout often decides performance more than algorithms do.
concepts.body:
Rule one: **measure**. Build with optimisations (`-O2`, plus `-march=native` for your exact CPU and `-flto`, link-time optimisation, which optimises across files, where suitable). Find where time goes with a **profiler** such as `perf`, VTune or Instruments, and time small pieces of code with a **benchmark** library like Google Benchmark, which stops the optimizer deleting your test. Intuition about performance is wrong surprisingly often.

Rule two: **memory dominates**. The CPU keeps recently used memory in small, fast caches. Reading main memory costs on the order of 100 ns (a **cache miss**), versus about 1 ns from the fastest cache, L1. The CPU fetches memory in 64-byte cache lines and, when you walk through memory in order, fetches the next lines in advance. So:

- Prefer contiguous containers. Iterating a `std::vector` is typically several times faster than a `std::list` or `std::map` of the same size, because every jump to the next separately stored element can be a cache miss. Sorted vectors and flat maps often beat trees and hash tables for small and medium sizes.
- Lay out data for how it's accessed. If a loop touches only positions, a **structure of arrays** (separate `x`, `y`, `z` vectors) keeps the cache full of useful bytes, where an array of structs drags whole objects in. Keep often-used members together and rarely used ones elsewhere.
- Avoid **false sharing**: two threads writing different variables that happen to sit on the same cache line make the cores pass that line back and forth. Pad per-thread data with `alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size)` (or 64).

Rule three: **don't do needless work**. `reserve()` before filling vectors; pass by `const&` or `string_view`; move instead of copying; avoid `std::function` and virtual calls in the hottest loops when templates or `std::variant` will do; keep allocation out of inner loops (use arenas, see allocators).

The CPU guesses which way each `if` will go and starts work early; a wrong guess, a **branch misprediction**, wastes about 15 clock cycles (the CPU's basic time step). Code without branches and predictable (for example sorted) data help, and C++20's `[[likely]]` / `[[unlikely]]` are hints. Finally, read the **assembly**, the human-readable form of the generated machine code (Compiler Explorer shows it), to confirm the optimizer did what you expect.
takeaways: Measure optimised builds with a profiler before changing anything
Contiguous, sequential data wins: cache misses cost ~100x a cache hit
Avoid needless allocations and copies; pad per-thread data against false sharing
pitfalls: Fine-tuning arithmetic while the real cost is cache misses from data spread across many separately allocated objects.

quiz.q: Two threads each increment their own counter, but the counters are adjacent members of one struct. Why can this scale poorly?
options: False sharing: both counters share a cache line that bounces between cores
quiz.explain: Writes from different cores to the same 64-byte line force the cores to keep handing the line back and forth, even though the data is distinct.

quiz.q: A physics loop reads only particle positions, but particles are stored as a vector of large structs. What layout change usually helps most?
options: Store positions in their own contiguous arrays (structure of arrays)
quiz.explain: A structure of arrays puts only the data the loop needs into the cache lines it pulls in, and lets the compiler process several values per instruction.
